# Omo Research

URL: https://www.omo.sh/

Omo Research explores voice-first AI, spatial agents, and local AI interfaces through focused questions, prototypes, and an open research log.

# The next interface isn't a chat window.

Agents now run for hours, a dozen at a time. We give each one a place, so you can find it, come back to it and see who needs you, the way you remember rooms.

---

# Omo Space: Real AI Agents at Desks in Minecraft

URL: https://www.omo.sh/omo-space

Omo Space gives every AI agent a room in Minecraft: walk to it to find it, come back to resume, glance down the hall. Real Hermes, Claude Code, Codex and shell sessions.

Abstract

People remember rooms better than tabs. Omo Space uses that: it gives every long-running agent a place in a shared 3D world, so finding one becomes walking to it, resuming becomes coming back to where you left it, and checking on the team becomes a glance down the hallway S6. It is a Minecraft mod and a small local service. Placing a computer block starts a named workspace on your own PC: a Hermes Agent conversation, a Claude Code or Codex session, or a plain shell. Its terminal is painted on a wall, real web pages run on monitors beside it, and a lamp shows whether it is working. Walking away, or quitting the game, stops nothing, because the sessions belong to a background session server, not to the game S1S2. This page describes what Omo Space is, how it is built, what survives what, what we built with it this week, and what it does not do yet. Version 1.2.0 was released on 28 October 2026 under the MIT licence S3S8.

01

## Introduction

Most agent interfaces disappear when you close the window. The agent is a tab, the tab looks like every other tab, and after a dozen of them it is hard to say which one is which, which one is working and which one is waiting for you.

From our streamA hall of desks with screens on the walls, 27 October

Omo Space starts from the opposite end. Each agent gets a place: a desk in a room, with its terminal on the wall and its name on a plate. You find it by walking to it. You check on it by looking down the hallway. When you come back the next day, it is where you left it S1.

Our companion paper, Rooms, Not Windows, reports five days of using it as a main workspace S6. This page is the system itself.

02

## What you can build

Everything is an ordinary-looking game block. The blocks below are the whole kit S1:

From our streamA real Hermes session on an in-world screen, answering live on stream

Block What it does

Hermes Computer One named workspace with a Hermes conversation in the profile you choose. Different agents, different desks.

Terminal A persistent shell. Its "+" menu opens Shell, Hermes, Claude Code or Codex tabs.

Omo Monitor / Slim Screen A bigger view of a terminal, or a real Chromium page: up to 6 tabs, its own sound, WASD for web games.

Omo Linker Mirrors a station onto walls across the room, with no wiring.

Omo Pocket A Hermes or Terminal workspace you carry as an item.

Name Plate / Status Lamp A name, and a live working / idle / interrupted light that also drives redstone.

Claude Code and Codex tabs are on the main branch and ship in the next release S3.

03

## How it works

The game is only the view. Four steps describe the whole interaction S1:

in the gameYou at a deskcomputer, pocket or wall

→

127.0.0.1 onlyLocal bridgepaints screens, sends keys

background servicetmux sessionsowns every workspace

your PCReal agentsHermes, Claude Code, Codex, shell

- Place a desk. A Hermes Computer or Terminal block opens a named workspace on your PC.

- Type on the wall. Your keys go to a real shell or agent, and its terminal is painted in the world.

- Walk away. tmux owns every session. Quit Minecraft and the work goes on while your PC is awake.

- Come back. It is on the wall where you left it. After a reboot, the desk reopens its tabs; nothing is re-run.

Underneath, a small bridge listens on 127.0.0.1 only. It paints the sessions onto in-game screens and sends your keystrokes back. The sessions themselves live in a tmux session server that runs as a background service S1S4.

Web walls are real Chromium pages. Since v1.2.0 a world can show 12 pages at once. A guard rate-limits new pages and closes all but the nearest walls if memory runs high, which fixed a crash where three walls kept evicting each other's page S3.

04

## What survives what

Persistence is the point, so it is worth being exact about it S2:

Stream clipReviewing a cut on the wall: the editing agent's work, where you left it

Event Shells and running jobs Hermes conversation

Close the screen, walk away Keep running Keeps running

Quit Minecraft Keep running Keeps running

Restart the bridge or launcher Keep running Keeps running

Hermes tab idle and unseen for 20 min (no change) Sleeps, saved, and resumes when a screen shows it

PC restart Lost; the tabs come back with the same names, shells in their last folder Saved, and resumes in its reopened tab

Two rules hold throughout. State is reported honestly: if the session server stops, the screen says INTERRUPTED. And nothing is re-run on its own: "Commands that were running are never re-run" S2.

05

## What we built with it this week

We use Omo Space as our main workspace, live on stream. Between 25 and 29 October 2026 the builder ran a content pipeline from inside the game, with one room per stage: ideas, references, recording requirements, editing, publishing and analytics. Each room has its own Hermes profile S6.

▶ Watch the 15-minute demo

Stream clipRooms going up, block by block, from one prompt

Stream clipAn underground lab, built from one prompt

From our streamA pipeline room: one stage, one agent, its work on the wall

From our streamThe planning wall in the underground base

From our streamAn AI agent joins the world as a player and follows you around

The rooms themselves were built by agents. The main underground base, with one room per stage, "Was done in one shot One prompt" S6. An underground robot lab was also built from one prompt, live on stream S1.

At the time of the companion paper, the bridge on the builder's machine reported 114 known workspaces, 62 live tmux sessions and 22 separate Hermes profiles. At peak he ran 21 to 25 agent sessions at once S6.

Since v1.2.0, agents running on the same computer can also join the world as players, over a LAN port that refuses offline logins from other machines S2S3. Our robots and the OMO agent player are built on that, and are described in Bodies in the Block World S7.

06

## Install

Download the installer, your platform's bundle and SHA256SUMS from the v1.2.0 release, check them, then install S1S8:

curl -LO https://github.com/omoresearch/omo-space/releases/download/v1.2.0/install.sh curl -LO https://github.com/omoresearch/omo-space/releases/download/v1.2.0/omo-research-1.2.0-linux-x64.tar.gz curl -LO https://github.com/omoresearch/omo-space/releases/download/v1.2.0/SHA256SUMS sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS bash install.sh omo-research-1.2.0-linux-x64.tar.gz

- The launcher fetches Minecraft 26.2, Fabric, CC: Tweaked, MCEF and Java from their official sources, with pinned hashes, into its own folder. It never touches your Minecraft or Prism installs.

- You need your own Minecraft Java account, Python 3.11+ and about 2 GB free. Hermes Agent is optional, and model access is your own.

- Setup fetches about 650 MB; the in-game browser fetches about 360 MB the first time a web wall opens.

- On Windows 10/11 the game runs natively, and the sessions and Hermes run in WSL2 (install.ps1).

07

## Security model

Omo Space puts real shells on your computer behind blocks in a world, so it should be treated with the same care as a terminal S4:

- The bridge listens on 127.0.0.1 only and refuses foreign Host headers.

- A computer's screen only ever holds a single-use ticket, bound to its station, its workspace and the running bridge.

- Worlds store workspace ids and monitor URLs, never a credential.

- Hermes' own approval prompts and permissions are untouched. Nothing here enables paid inference by itself.

It is for singleplayer and trusted local worlds. "A block, a room or a pocket dimension is a presentation boundary, not a sandbox." S4

08

## Limitations

From our streamPart of our world, 27 October

- Platforms. Tested end to end on Linux. macOS and Windows support is new and tested offline only; a clean-machine install through Microsoft sign-in has not been tested yet S1S5.

- Desk agents do not act in the world. "A Hermes desk agent does not act in the world. It cannot walk, place blocks or press buttons." Agent bodies are a separate runtime S2.

- Agents do not talk to each other through the world. Work is handed between them the normal Hermes way S2.

- Workspaces live on the PC that opened them. A friend on another PC gets a fresh workspace from the same preset S2.

- Web video. The bundled Chromium has no H.264/AAC codecs, so YouTube plays but most Instagram, X and Reddit video does not S1.

- The game is heavier than the work. In our own use, the game client crashed or froze more often than the agent sessions failed; the sessions survived S6.

09

# Worlds, Not Windows: Spatial Agentic Interfaces

URL: https://www.omo.sh/papers/worlds-not-windows

Findings so far from using Omo Space every day: AI agent sessions and live web pages given places in a Minecraft world. By Harrison Edwards, Omo Research.

Worlds, Not Windows: Spatial Agentic Interfaces | Omo Research

Omo Research← PapersWhitepaperPDF (paper)PDF (whitepaper)

Omo Research · preprint draft v1.830 October 2026

# Worlds, Not Windows

Spatially Aware Creative Agentic Interfaces

Harrison Edwards

Omo Research

Working paper · draft v1.8 · November 2026

Figure 1. Worlds, not windows. An organisation drawn as an open world of districts, with agents at work in each and all of them linked to a central status wall. Generated illustration (Omo Space enterprise site), not a screenshot; captures from Minecraft appear in Figures 3–5.

Abstract. AI agents now run for hours, many at a time, yet we still manage them through chat windows and terminal tabs. With twenty agents running, the tab bar stops telling you which agent is which and which one needs you. We tried something else: we gave each agent session a place in a Minecraft world. Omo Space is a mod that puts real agent sessions (Hermes Agent, Claude Code) and live web pages on in-world screens, with lamps that show when an agent is working. The sessions themselves keep running on the user’s computer, and the places are mostly built by coding agents from short requests. This paper shares findings so far from the builder using it himself. He worked in it every day while streaming (25–29 October 2026), and a friend built his own world with it. Looking back over about 29 hours of transcribed streams, we describe four ways place got used: to find work by walking to it, to resume by coming back to it, to monitor by glancing at lit screens, and to orchestrate a pipeline by moving work from place to place. We also report his real usage from the agents’ own logs: about 7 billion tokens over the five days, and over 4 billion on 28 October alone. We have not tested it against tabs; we describe what it was like, what it suggests, and what we would like to measure next.

Keywords: agentic interfaces; spatial interfaces; persistence; ambient awareness; multi-agent supervision; generative environments; Minecraft; autobiographical design

## 1 Introduction

AI agents have gone from one chat to many long-running sessions: coding agents, research agents, video-editing agents. They work for hours, wait for approval and ask questions. Most of us still run them in chat windows or terminal tabs. That works for one agent. With twenty, the tab bar no longer tells you which session is which, which one is busy, and which one is waiting for you.

The builder of the system in this paper put the motivation this way, on the first night of streaming it:

“So it’s like I’m spatially aware of my workspace. … It’s not a chat window, it’s an interface.”[P1, T1, 00:38:33–00:38:50, live]

Using space to organise computer work is an old idea. Rooms (1986) split a crowded screen into virtual rooms [1], Data Mountain (1998) showed people remember where they put things in 3D [2], and the Task Gallery (2000) hung running applications on gallery walls [3]. Agents are a new kind of thing to organise. They keep working when you look away, they finish, and they ask for help. We wanted to know what a world of places does for that kind of work, and what it does not do.

What this paper is. Findings so far, from one person building and using his own tool. Nothing here was set up as a test. The builder just used Omo Space for his real work, live on stream, and a friend tried it too. We went back through the recordings and wrote down what happened, in his own words, including what went wrong. We do not claim the world is faster than tabs; Section 7 lists what we would like to measure next.

We contribute:

- A system. Omo Space, which shows live agent sessions and web pages as objects in a Minecraft world, with status lamps and agent-built places (§3).

- Findings so far. Five days of the builder’s own daily use, about 29 hours of stream transcripts, read with AI helpers and checked by script (§4).

- What we learned. Four uses of place, the “web page with a terminal attached” pattern, places at every scale and a traced episode (§5).

- What to do next. Design lessons and what we would like to measure next (§6–7).

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Space, memory and interruption

Malone found that piles on a desk do more than store things: “a very important function of desk organization is to remind the user of things to do” [4]. Rooms carried this into software with virtual workspaces, to cut “window thrashing” [1]. Data Mountain reported “statistically reliable advantages” for placing documents in space over a favourites list [2]. The Task Gallery, which hosted ordinary Windows applications in 3D, was found “enjoyable to use” [3]. People juggle many tasks and find switching hard [6], and they use spatial memory to return to “the general area where they were interrupted” [7]. Calm technology argues for displays that show state “without being obtrusive” [5]. All of this was about documents, windows and tasks; none of it was about supervising agents that keep working on their own.

### 2.2 Agents in game worlds

Minecraft is a common home for AI agents. Voyager explores and learns skills [8], Mindcraft studies agent teams and finds communication is a main bottleneck [10], and Generative Agents fills a game town with twenty-five agents people can watch and talk to [9]. In those systems the world is mostly where the agents act. In Omo Space the world is mainly the human’s view of, and controls for, agents whose real work (code, video, publishing) happens outside the game. The line is not sharp, since Generative Agents is also something people watch.

### 2.3 Supervising many agents

The closest recent work tackles the same problem with dashboards. ParallelPilot adds planning, a run-logger and “an ambient dashboard alongside existing coding tools”; in a study with 16 people, participants “supervised an average of one more concurrent agent at peak” [19]. AgentGUI is built for “observing and steering AI agents amid multiple concurrent, long-running sessions” [20]. Magentic-UI offers “co-planning, co-tasking, multi-tasking, action guards, and long-term memory” [21]. Generative UI shows models can generate “not just the content, but the interface itself” [22]. Spatial hypertext found that “a visual/spatial metaphor … allows people to express the nuances of structure” [23]. Table 0 compares them. What Omo Space adds is a combination: places, built by people or agents, that hold long-running sessions and agent-made pages. Unlike ParallelPilot and AgentGUI it has not been tested with users. Unlike Magentic-UI it has no action guards. And unlike ParallelPilot’s dashboard, which surfaces intervention cues, its lamps show activity but not “this agent is waiting for you”.

Table 0. Omo Space and the nearest systems, as described in the material we inspected (mostly abstracts and introductions). “n/i” means not established from the inspected source; it does not mean the feature is absent.

SystemConcurrent sessionsWhere jobs run; persistenceState / intervention cuesGenerated interfaceSpatial organisationEvaluation (task)

ParallelPilot [19]YesExisting coding tools; n/iAmbient dashboard; intervention cuesn/in/iWithin-subjects N=16 (short coding tickets)

AgentGUI [20]Yes, long-runningLocally hosted; n/iTrace visualisation; steeringn/in/iControlled study (finding key elements in traces)

Magentic-UI [21]Multi-taskingWeb, code, files; n/iAction guards; co-planningn/in/iBenchmarks, simulated users, qualitative study, safety tests

Generative UI [22]n/in/in/iCustom pages per promptn/iHuman preference ratings

VIKI [23]n/in/in/in/iUser-arranged 2D spacen/i

Task Gallery [3]ApplicationsUnmodified Windows appsn/in/i3D gallery (authored)User studies

Omo SpaceYestmux on user’s machine; survives client exitLamps, lit screens; no waiting statePages and placesGenerated places, any scaleNone yet (findings from own use)

### 2.4 How we looked back at it

Building a tool and learning from your own use of it has a name in HCI, autobiographical design: “design research drawing on extensive, genuine usage by those creating or building a system” [16], with an autoethnographic flavour [18]. We borrow the steps of thematic analysis [15]. Because AI models did the first reading, we call it an AI-assisted thematic synthesis rather than a full reflexive analysis. AI coding has matched experts reasonably well when there is a fixed codebook [17], but ours was open-ended, so we also checked the outputs by script (§4.3).

## 3 System: Omo Space

Omo Space is a Fabric mod for Minecraft Java 26.2 plus a small local bridge [11][12]. We describe it from source snapshot 75d4677 (27 Oct 2026); the builds used day to day were not recorded. At the time it ran on Linux only [11].

### 3.1 What is in the world

A workspace is a named terminal session (tmux) on the user’s computer. It has one or more tabs, each running an agent (Hermes, Claude Code, Codex) or a plain shell. Each Hermes agent has its own profile: memory, skills and model. In the world, a station is the computer block for a workspace. Views (wall monitors, slim screens) show a tab or a live web page, and several views can show the same workspace. A place is anything you build around them: a room, a cave, a tower, a world. Places are just builds; they carry no permissions and run nothing.

Table 1. In-world objects and their counterparts on the user’s machine [11].

ObjectCounterpart on the machine

Hermes Computer (station)A named workspace whose first tab runs a Hermes agent in its own profile

TerminalA workspace tab running a shell or another agent CLI

Monitor wall / Slim ScreenA larger view of a tab, or a pinned live web page (embedded Chromium)

LinkerBinds a view to a workspace without adjacency; several views may mirror one

Status LampFollows an explicitly linked station, or else the nearest station within 8 blocks. Gold if any live tab in the workspace is busy, green otherwise, red once interrupted, dark without a live workspace

Name PlateThe workspace name, legible at a distance

A lamp sums up its workspace: gold if any tab is busy, otherwise green (source: StationStatus.glow). It has no “waiting for your answer” state. Agents do not pass work to each other through the world, and a friend loading the same map gets fresh workspaces of their own [11]. So a pipeline that runs across places is the user’s own scripts and agent instructions, not something the mod does.

Figure 2. Architecture. Processes are owned by a tmux server on the user’s machine. A loopback-only bridge renders tabs onto in-world screens and forwards input. The client presents and accepts input but does not own the external agent jobs.

### 3.2 What survives what

Each Hermes tab is one named conversation (hermes -p <profile> chat --tui -c omo:<workspace>:<tab>), so reopening a screen brings back the same conversation [11]. Closing a screen, quitting Minecraft or restarting the bridge does not stop the agents. Restarting the computer does stop running jobs, but saved conversations can be resumed with a button. Idle Hermes tabs nap after 20 minutes unseen and wake when shown again; apart from that, “Nothing is ever re-run without you” [11].

Table 2. Documented lifecycle by event [11]; documented behaviour, not a survival test run for this paper. World layout is saved by Minecraft. Web-page state on a wall is not covered by this table,.

EventShells and running jobsHermes conversation

Close the view, walk awayKeep runningKeeps running

Quit or crash MinecraftKeep runningKeeps running

Restart the bridgeKeep runningKeeps running

Hermes tab idle and unseen 20 min—Exits cleanly; resumes when shown

Host restart, or tmux server stopsLostSaved; tab shows INTERRUPTED; user presses Resume

(a) Terminal + web wall

(b) Review wall

Figure 3. Agent work as objects in a place. (a) A Hermes session on a wall terminal (right) beside other agents’ walls across the room. (b) An agent-built review page pinned on a wall: a queue of clips “ready to review” with a player and notes. Stills from the authors’ live stream of 30 Oct 2026 (recordings 2026-10-30 05-26-05 and 23-31-03), the day after the five days covered here, in the live world with real agent sessions. Frames are cropped to remove the face camera, stream label and game HUD.

### 3.3 Places built by agents

Places can be built and changed by coding agents from plain requests, and people also build by hand. Agents can also have bodies: a companion project brings a Hermes-driven player into the same world [13], and simulated robots appear in it. Bodies are outside the scope of this paper.

## 4 How We Looked Back

### 4.1 Who used it

From 25 to 29 October 2026 the builder (P1), a solo developer, simply used Omo Space as his main workspace while streaming to Twitch and YouTube. There was no study plan; the streams were his normal work. He ran a real content pipeline (ideas, references, recording, editing, publishing, analytics) with about one agent profile per stage, linked by his own scripts. A friend (P2), new to Hermes and on Windows, built his own world from the public repository with help from Claude Code and showed it on two streams. We did not inspect P2’s code; his set-up time and how easy he found it are his own account (§5.7).

### 4.2 Data

We used seven main stream recordings and four short pickups, transcribed with Whisper (small), with a timestamp on every line. We split them into eight segments (Table 3), 29.05 hours in total. That figure is computed by corpus_manifest.py from the first and last timestamp in each analysed range. It includes silence, chat and replayed clips, so it is recorded time, not hours of distinct events. Two stretches were not analysed: the first 93 minutes of the 28 October part-2 recording (only partly transcribed) and 29 October after 3 h 44 min (not yet transcribed). The transcripts have no speaker labels, so who said what is inferred from context throughout. For P2 we also mark it at each quote.

Table 3. Corpus and extraction yield per segment. Counts are extracted records, not distinct events; repeated clips and scripted takes can yield several records.

Seg.Recording (2026)HoursThesesQuotesDemos

T125 Oct, 02:08 (first stream)2.80175918

T225 Oct, 18:56 + pickups (incl. 26 Oct)1.99156017

T325 Oct, 23:413.90175514

T427 Oct, 18:033.77175925

T528 Oct, 01:36, 0:00–4:404.65166420

T628 Oct, 01:36, 4:40–9:204.67185423

T728 Oct, 11:40, 1:33–5:073.57165921

T829 Oct, 16:19, 0:00–3:443.70175918

Total29.05133469156

### 4.3 Real usage

The streams show what was said. Hermes also keeps its own token counters for every session, so we can say how much agent work actually ran (Table 4). Over the five days the builder’s agents used about 7.1 billion tokens in 43,157 model calls. On 28 October alone they used about 4.2 billion; counting only sessions that started and ended that day it is still 3.75 billion. The day after the five days, 30 October, was busier again at 4.7 billion, with 20 agent profiles active. By 29 October twelve profiles were running, roughly one per pipeline stage.

Most of these tokens are context being re-read, not new text. From 24 October to 1 November, 95.7% were cache reads: each step of a long-running agent re-reads its whole conversation from the provider’s prompt cache. Output was 66 million tokens (0.5%). Nearly all of it (99.3%) ran on Claude Opus 5.5. At list prices Hermes estimates the five days at about $3,400; no billed cost is recorded, so this is an equivalent, not what was paid. The counters cover all of the builder’s Hermes work, including sessions that never appeared in the world, so they measure how much agent work he was running, not how much Omo Space caused. The script and per-day data are in the project’s usage/ folder.

Table 4. Real usage, from Hermes’ own per-session token counters across all 45 local profile databases (read 1 Nov 2026). Days in AEDT; sessions that ran past midnight are split by time. The sessions column includes sub-agents and scheduled jobs. Cost is Hermes’ estimate at published list prices, not an invoice.

DayTokensAPI callsAgent profilesSessionsList-price estimate

Sat 25 Oct0.09 bn970333$32

Sun 26 Oct0.63 bn5,0049137$311

Mon 27 Oct0.56 bn3,989994$323

Tue 28 Oct4.17 bn25,38611537$1,978

### 4.4 Analysis

Reading. Each segment was read in full by a separate AI reader (Claude Opus 5.5). Each listed the claims made about the interface with 1–4 exact timestamped quotes each, the live demos, the failures and doubts, and guest reactions. All readers shared one brief. That brief asked what the builder was “trying to SAY/PROVE” and gave example claims, so it was looking for his intent, and may have nudged the readers (full prompts: Appendix A).

Grouping. An AI drafting assistant (also Claude) grouped the 133 segment-level claims into cross-segment themes. P1 checked the result against what he meant. No second person coded the material. The theme list, its rules and coverage counts are in Appendix C as an index; the findings below do not rest on the counts.

Labels on quotes. Each quote is tagged live (said while working), take (a scripted promo line recorded in the world) or playback (an edited clip replayed on stream). Takes show what P1 wanted to say, not what happened. Even live quotes are reports of what someone said, not observed outcomes. We worked from transcripts, not video.

Checks. A script confirmed that all 791 quotes the readers extracted appear in the transcripts within 3 minutes of their timestamps. A second, stricter script checks every quote in this paper against its own segment’s transcript within 90 seconds. On v1.8 it found 30 timed matches and no failures, and it matched 14 literature quotes against the fetched sources (Appendix B). These checks show the words are there; they do not prove who said them or what happened. Key moments have not yet been checked against the audio.

### 4.5 Privacy and consent

The streams were public, and P1 is the system’s author. Figures 3–5 are stream stills cropped so that no face camera, chat, viewer names or stream labels show. P2 has a pseudonym here, but the working files name him and his words can be found in the public recordings. He is not named here, and everything quoted was said on public streams.

## 5 What We Found

We read the material through four uses of place: find, resume, monitor and orchestrate. They are how we make sense of what happened, not proven effects. Table 5 sums them up; the sections after it give the evidence. Then come the “web page with a terminal” pattern, places at every scale, and P2’s world.

Table 5. The four uses of place at a glance. Each row: what it looked like, what the builders said helped, and the lesson we draw.

UseWhat it looked likeWhat helped (reported)Lesson

FindWalk to the agent’s placeRemembering places, not tab positions; about 25 sessions at oncePlaces help find work if they stay put and stay legible

ResumeCome back to where you left itAgents still running after quitting the gameThe place is an address; each kind of state needs its own guarantee

MonitorGlance at lit screens and lampsScreens “turn on” when an agent works (T8, 00:48:43, live)Activity and “waiting for you” are different signals

OrchestrateMove work from place to placePipeline stages visible as roomsSpace is not routing; hand-offs need to be explicit

(a) Find

(b) Resume

(c) Monitor

(d) Orchestrate

Figure 4. What each use of place looks like in the world. (a) Find: a corridor of places, each with its own screen. (b) Resume: a hall of agent places in the underground base he worked in every day. (c) Monitor: lit screens readable from the cavern entrance. (d) Orchestrate: the review stage of the video pipeline, with approve / send back / move to done controls, beside the editing agent’s terminal. Stills from the authors’ live stream of 30 Oct 2026 (recordings 2026-10-30 05-26-05 and 23-31-03), the day after the five days covered here, in the live world with real agent sessions. Frames are cropped to remove the face camera, stream label and game HUD. The images illustrate layout; they do not show interaction outcomes.

### 5.1 Find: walking to the work

Every workspace sits in a fixed, named place, so you can remember where an agent is instead of which tab it was in. P1 put it most sharply in a scripted take:

“Nobody remembers which of the 12 terminal tabs are doing what but you can remember space and rooms … It’s the oldest memory trick out there.”[P1, T6, 07:14:29–07:14:46, take]

Live, he named the problem the world was built to fix: “Getting lost with all these tabs and things” [T1, 01:13:45, live]. He reported about 25 sessions running at once (the logs show 537 sessions active on 28 October, counting sub-agents and scheduled jobs), “within the interface that we can conceptually understand” [T6, 07:37:22, live]. Whether the spatial-memory gains seen for documents [2] carry over to live agents is something we would like to measure (H1).

### 5.2 Resume: coming back to it

The agents run outside the game (Table 2), so leaving the game does not stop them, and the places are still there when you return. After quitting and reloading on the first night P1 said: “So we can close it enjoy our day And then Come back Boom the agents are still working right here” [T1, 02:12:55, live]. On 29 October he said agents had kept editing after he closed Minecraft, about 22 clips [T8, 00:06:30–00:08:38, live]. Separately, after turning the computer off and on, he found “everything’s persistent” [T8, 00:11:55–00:11:59, live]. A restart keeps the world and the saved conversations but not running jobs (Table 2), so we read these as two separate moments, not as work done while the computer was off. He tied this to how it felt to start work: “I’m not dreading any pain / Or like context loss because I know anytime I want to work on the robotics project / I just fly down here” [T4, 02:21:42, live].

### 5.3 Monitor: glancing at lit screens

Lamps and lit screens let you read activity from across the room, much like calm technology [5]. P1’s clearest lines are takes recorded in the Batcave: “because every light that you see in there is an agent still working” [T5, 00:36:26, take] and “Now you can see your whole team from the hallway.” [T5, 00:39:00, take]. P2 described the same cue live, in his own world: “How I can tell when the task is like running because their screen will turn on” [T8, 00:48:43, live; P2, inferred]. He also said watching the team was more fun than “just looking at you know Claude you know just typing” [T8, 01:00:57, live; P2, inferred].

The lamps show who is busy. They do not yet show that an agent is waiting for an answer, and that is the next signal to build (H3).

### 5.4 Orchestrate: moving work between places

P1 laid out his content pipeline as a row of places, about one stage and one agent each: “We just go to that room and just start building / And when we’re done, then we just leave that room” [T2, 01:04:14, live]. In a take he summed it up: “This video went through all five rooms before you saw it” [T5, 00:34:55, take]. By 29 October he wanted a place for each to-do item, “a repeatable pattern” [T8, 03:28:22, live]. In conversation, approving was described as a single in-world step: “once you press approve inside the game, it just gets posted” [T8, 00:56:28, live; speaker unclear].

The hand-offs between places are his own scripts and agent instructions, not a feature of the mod. Laying the pipeline out in space made its stages visible and easy to visit.

### 5.5 Web pages with a terminal attached

On the last day P1 described the idea in its most general form, apart from Minecraft:

“the concept of spatial interfaces with persistent webpages is easy to use and talk to and control. … We’re doing it inside Minecraft, but I believe there is not enough … attention, these persistent webpages with a terminal attached to it. And with this, you can build whatever pipeline that you want.”[P1, T8, 03:38:57–03:39:18, live]

Pieced together from several moments, the pattern goes like this. You ask an agent at a station for a page for one job, such as a review queue, an analytics view or a publishing form. You pin it on a wall in the right place, check it, and approve or ask for changes through the terminal next to it. Then you come back to it later. The page does the job-specific work; the place gives it a fixed home next to related work. An ordinary browser tab could host the same page, and we did not separate the two effects. The in-world browser also had limits: drop-down menus could not be selected [T8, 03:22:45, live]. The episode below shows one piece of it on the first night.

Episode A: leave and return (T1, 02:10:30–02:13:16; live; reports). Set-up. P1 pins a web page on a wall beside working agents: “And then I get pins page to forever be here” [T1, 02:10:40]. Action. He closes the world: “I’m closing it entirely” [T1, 02:12:03]. Result as reported. On reloading: “Boom the agents are still working right here” [T1, 02:13:04], and “Web page is still here” [T1, 02:13:12]. What it shows. The agent sessions’ survival matches the documented lifecycle (Table 2). The pinned page was there too.

### 5.6 Places at every scale

The places were not just rooms. P1 ran his content pipeline through a cave of five rooms. He wanted whole worlds for lines of work: “We can build a whole world for the paid ads” [T7, 02:48:38, live]. To show how personal it could get, he imagined a pirate ship holding your tax work [T6, 08:09:08, live]. He said agents did most of the building: “I didn’t build any of this” [T6, 07:45:10, live]. He also liked building by hand sometimes: “I also think it’s quite nice to just build with hand” [T1, 02:25:32, live]. The pattern is that people choose the shape and size of a place to fit the work, instead of the system choosing for them.

(a) Atrium

(b) Hall

(c) White hall

(d) Tunnel

Figure 5. Places at several scales in the authors’ world, from a single atrium to halls and the tunnels that connect them. In (b) an embodied agent (name tag “ChatGPT – …”) stands in the hall. The authors report that these places were generated by agents from short requests; per-build prompts were not logged. Stills from the authors’ live stream of 30 Oct 2026 (recordings 2026-10-30 05-26-05 and 23-31-03), the day after the five days covered here, in the live world with real agent sessions. Frames are cropped to remove the face camera, stream label and game HUD.

### 5.7 A friend’s world

This part comes from what was said during P2’s screen-share, not from watching the video. P2 had never used Hermes before [T8, 00:59:38] and described about 24 hours of work [T8, 00:54:32] with little troubleshooting: “It just gave Claude the GitHub and then gave it a few prompts and then it just it built the world” [T8, 01:04:44, live; P2, inferred]. He showed an AI office with a manager agent, teams for web, social and IT, and a podium for talking to the whole team. Agents walked to their seats at a conference table, and a sports arena showed live scores [T8, 00:28–01:13]. The manager, seating and podium were his own additions, not part of Omo Space; they show a second builder taking the idea his own way. Someone in the exchange described a meeting table where a message “will go to each of the four people’s like memories and sessions” [T8, 01:12:04, live]; the transcript does not show who said it or whose table it was. The day before, P2 had called a page-only setup “claustrophobic” [T7, 04:16:50, live; P2, inferred].

## 6 Discussion

### 6.1 Design implications

- Give agent work a persistent, recognisable place, while allowing several sessions per place, mirrored views and user-chosen scales.

- Separate address from state: state the persistence of process, conversation, page and world separately (Table 2).

- Distinguish activity from a request for attention, without colour as the only cue.

- Honest state: never show progress that is not happening; re-run nothing on the user’s behalf except documented idle resume.

- Let the work choose the shape: places of any scale, built by agents or by hand.

- Make hand-offs between places explicit objects, not a consequence of layout.

### 6.2 Why a game world, and why people liked it

Earlier 3D workspaces were designed by their makers [3]. A buildable world lets agents make the places from requests and lets other people build their own. That is what gave us places at every scale (§5.6) and P2’s world (§5.7).

Both builders also chose where to work and said they liked being there. P1 described moving between reading and coding: “I can uh, read and then I can go to the other room … Do some coding or whatever and then go back to like reading and it’s all together in one place in my mind” [T3, 02:01:07–02:01:11, live]. P2 said watching the team “makes this like AI coding and building stuff just more fun” [T8, 01:00:57, live; P2, inferred]. These are claims about how it felt, not wellbeing results.

### 6.3 Limitations

- Just us so far. One builder using his own tool, and one friend. Nothing was set up as a test, there is no comparison and nothing was measured. These are lessons from use, not proof that worlds beat tabs.

- The builder is the author. P1 built the system and was streaming, and some key lines are promo takes or replayed clips (§4.3). Studying your own system shows a lot but leans toward your own needs [16].

- Analysis. AI models did the reading and grouping, and P1 checked them. There was no second human coder.

- Transcripts. Whisper (small), no speaker labels. One line reads “I don’t think Minecraft is superior” (T6, 08:33:45). It may be misheard, but until someone listens to the audio we leave it open.

- Coverage. About 29 hours analysed; two stretches were not (§4.2).

- Pictures. The figures show what the interface looks like, not results. Figures 3–5 are stills from 30 October, the day after the five days covered here; Figure 1 is a generated illustration.

## 7 What We Would Like to Measure Next

None of this has been tested yet. If we do test it, three of the four uses can be compared against ordinary tabs, and generated places can be looked at from logs (Table 6). The comparison must be fair. The tab setup gets the same agents, the same persistence, good names, status badges and search, so any difference comes from space and not from better tools. Orchestration waits until hand-offs between places are real features.

Table 6. Proposed studies. H1–H3 are within-subjects and counterbalanced. Sample size is provisional (about 16–24) pending a pilot and power analysis. H4 is an observational log study.

StudyPredictionManipulationMeasure

H1 FindNamed sessions are located faster in the world than in tabs, and the gap widens with session count.Interface (world, tabs) × sessions (12, 24)Time to locate; wrong selections

H2 ResumeAfter a 24 h break, time to first useful action is shorter in the world.Interface; 24 h delay; “useful action” defined in advanceResumption lag; errors

H3 MonitorWith a proposed “waiting for you” lamp state (not yet built), a blocked session is noticed sooner than with equivalent tab badges when it is in view, but not when out of view unless escalation is added.Interface × visibility (in view: same room / visible tab strip; out of view: other room / other workspace) × escalation (off, on); identical event schedule in bothDetection latency; misses (unnoticed within 5 min)

H4 Build (obs.)Most one-prompt places are used without post-generation revisions.None; log every build attempt (failed and abandoned included) started in days 1–30, each followed for 14 days (observation ends day 44)Author acceptance; still in use after 14 days; revisions; independent usability rating against a pre-registered checklist

“Useful action” in H2 means the first edit, approval or instruction that moves the interrupted task forward. Participants practise each interface until they complete two trials unaided, and task versions are matched by session count and event schedule. In H4, a “one-prompt” place is one plain request with no follow-up, and any later edit the user asks for, by hand or by agent, counts as a revision. Some of the data already exists: bridge logs of sleep, resume and INTERRUPTED events, the Hermes session stores, and the recordings.

## 8 Conclusion

Chat windows were made for one conversation; agent work is now many conversations that keep going when you look away. We gave that work places in a world you can build, from a single room up to whole worlds. Its builder described finding, resuming, watching and routing agent work by moving through those places, and a friend took the idea his own way. Whether worlds help people more than windows is still an open question; §7 sketches how we would like to find out.

## Data and Materials

The per-segment extractions, reader prompts, synthesis, theme matrix (theme_matrix.py), corpus manifest (corpus_manifest.py), quotation verifiers (verify_quotes.py, verify_paper_quotes.py), citation ledger with verbatim evidence and the review history are held in the project folder. They are not a public release: they contain identifying material about P2 and other speakers. A redacted evidence subset will be prepared before any release. Raw recordings are not released.

## AI Use Disclosure

Language-model readers (Claude) performed first-pass extraction. A language-model assistant (Claude) proposed the cross-segment themes, coverage counts and the text of this draft, which P1 reviewed. An independent model (GPT-6 Astra) reviewed the draft against the evidence files and the full drafting history; its review is kept with the project materials. Stream quotations were checked by script against transcripts (Appendix B), and literature quotations against fetched source text in the citation ledger. Those checks cover the existence of the words, not interpretation. The thesis-to-theme matrix in Appendix C was reconstructed by the drafting assistant after review.

## Appendix A. Reader Prompts

The eight reader prompts (one shared brief plus a per-segment assignment) are archived verbatim in stream-analysis/READER-PROMPTS.json, recovered from the session store. The shared brief asks the reader to read the assigned range completely and extract: (1) theses, i.e. every claim the builder is “trying to demonstrate/prove about the interface”, with examples given; (2) 1–4 verbatim quotations per thesis with line timestamps; (3) live demonstrations; (4) counter-evidence and friction, including sceptical guest reactions; (5) guest and viewer reactions; and (6) memorable phrasings. It asks for honesty when a chunk is unrelated and says “Never invent quotes or timestamps”. These are instructions; compliance was checked only for quotation existence (Appendix B). The example theses in the brief may have primed the readers.

## Appendix B. Quotation Verification

Corpus check. verify_quotes.py normalises each quotation record from the readers’ theses, friction and phrasings (lowercase, punctuation stripped except apostrophes, whitespace collapsed, split on ellipses). It requires the fragments in order within ±180 s of the stated time. Result, first run 29 Oct 2026 and re-run by the reviewer on 30 Oct: 791 of 791 matched. Limits: T2 pickups are pooled, records without a parsable time are searched without a window, and speakers and live/replay status are not checked.

Paper check. verify_paper_quotes.py detects selected main-text quotations (curly-quoted spans before the References) and checks their text near the supplied locators. It requires every fragment, split on ellipses and “ / ”, to occur in order in the stated segment’s own transcript, between 90 s before the earliest and 90 s after the latest time in the locator. T2 pickups are resolved by file name. A listed set of scare-quoted terms in our own voice is skipped. Literature excerpts are matched against the pooled fetched source texts and cited local documentation. This is not a check of attribution to a specific reference; that was done by hand and is recorded with evidence in ledger.json. Result on v1.8 is recorded in the study README.

## Appendix C. Thesis-to-Theme Matrix (reconstructed)

Files. theme_matrix.py holds the rules, the mapping and the change log, and checks without writing. --write regenerates stream-analysis/THEME-MATRIX.json; the input is restricted to the eight segment files. Current matrix: 133 enumerated theses; 117 linked to at least one theme; 16 unlinked; 137 links. The first-pass reconstruction is kept as theme_matrix_v1.py.

Changes in the second pass. T8-8 (one-prompt delegation of websites, ads and clips) was removed from C7 because no place is built. T8-5 (P2’s world “built” by Claude from the repository) was added to C7. T6 T15 (an observation deck and feeling safe) was removed from C5 because no agent state is read. T3-11 (gamified, fun work) was moved from C12 to C13. T1-5 was added to C5, because C5 includes proposals. Five theses were added to C13. Net effect against the first pass: C5 8→7, C12 5→4, C13 new at 5; C7 unchanged at 7, now resting on T8-5 rather than T8-8.

Worked positive case. T6 thesis T2 (strength 5), “Rooms, not tabs: spatial memory … beats remembering which of N terminal tabs does what”, with quotation [T6, 07:14:29, take], meets the C1 rule.

Worked boundary case. T1-5 (strength 4), “Reading text in chat boxes causes fatigue … wants visual, glanceable or voice output”. It meets C4 (reading fatigue) and, because C5 counts proposals, C5. Under a use-only reading it would leave C5; that would not change C5’s count, because T1 has other qualifying theses.

Fragility. The script lists every cell where dropping one link lowers a theme’s count; for example, C7 in T8 rests only on T8-5, and C10 in T1 only on T1-10. The negative case in the corpus (“I don’t think Minecraft is superior”, T6 08:33:45) is a separate, unresolved ASR question, not part of this matrix.

Excluding C11 (a product claim), seven themes appear in at least seven of eight segments; four of them sit at exactly 7/8 and depend on single links in at least one segment.

# Worlds, Not Windows · Omo Research whitepaper

URL: https://www.omo.sh/papers/worlds-not-windows/whitepaper

Worlds, Not Windows. Spatially aware creative agentic interfaces: findings so far, from daily use of Omo Space.

## 01The problem

AI agents no longer answer one question and stop. They run for hours. They write code, cut video, draft posts and wait for approval. And we run many of them at once.

Most of us still manage them through chat windows and terminal tabs. That works for one agent. It mostly works for three. With twenty, the tab bar stops telling you the things you need to know. Which session is which? Which one is busy? Which one finished an hour ago? Which one is stuck, waiting for you?

A tab is a label in a row of labels. It looks the same whether the agent behind it is working hard, done, or blocked on a question. You find out by clicking through them, one by one.

On the first night of streaming with Omo Space, Harrison put the alternative like this:

“So it’s like I’m spatially aware of my workspace. … It’s not a chat window, it’s an interface.” [T1, 00:38:33–00:38:50, live]

## 02The idea: worlds, not windows

Our idea is simple. Give agent work a place. Not a tab, not a window, but somewhere you can walk to.

People are good at remembering where things are. We remember which room the books are in and which shelf holds the tools. We are much worse at remembering that the video agent was the seventh tab from the left. So instead of a row of tabs, we put each agent session in a place in a world, with a screen you can read and a lamp that shows when it is working.

Places come at every scale. A single room for one job. A cave of rooms for a whole content pipeline. A tower, an office, an arena. A whole world for one line of work. The shape is chosen to fit the work, not imposed by the software.

And the places do not have to be built by hand. In Omo Space, coding agents build most of them from short requests. You ask for a place and an agent builds it. That changes the cost of a spatial interface: making a new room is closer to opening a new folder than to building a level in a game.

IllustrationThe idea at its largest scale: an organisation drawn as an open world of districts, with agents at work in each. A generated illustration, not a screenshot. It shows where we would like to go, not what we have seen.

## 03How Omo Space works

Omo Space is a Fabric mod for Minecraft Java 26.2, plus a small local bridge. It puts real agent sessions (Hermes Agent and Claude Code) and live web pages on screens inside the game.

The key design choice: the game does not run the agents. Each workspace is a named terminal session (tmux) on the user’s own computer. It has one or more tabs, each running an agent or a plain shell. A bridge that listens only on the local machine paints those sessions onto in-world screens and sends your keys back. Minecraft is the view and the controls. The work lives outside it.

In the worldWhat it is on the computer

Hermes ComputerA named workspace whose first tab runs a Hermes agent in its own profile (its own memory, skills and model)

TerminalA workspace tab running a shell or another agent CLI

Monitor wall / Slim ScreenA larger view of a tab, or a pinned live web page

LinkerBinds a screen to a workspace from a distance; several screens can mirror one

Status LampGold if any tab in the workspace is busy, green when idle, red once interrupted, dark with no live workspace

Name PlateThe workspace name, readable from across the room

A place is anything you build around these objects: a room, a cave, a tower, a world. Places are just builds. They carry no permissions and run nothing.

### What survives what

Because the agents live in tmux, not in the game, closing things in the game does not stop them. Each Hermes tab is one named conversation, so reopening a screen brings back the same conversation, not a new one.

What happensRunning jobsHermes conversation

Close the screen, walk awayKeep runningKeeps running

Quit or crash MinecraftKeep runningKeeps running

Restart the bridgeKeep runningKeeps running

Hermes tab idle and unseen 20 min—Naps; wakes when shown again

Restart the PCStoppedSaved; tab shows INTERRUPTED; press Resume

So a PC restart does stop running work. Saved conversations come back with a button. Nothing re-runs on its own: in the documentation’s words, “Nothing is ever re-run without you” [1]. This table is the documented behaviour. Web pages pinned on walls are a separate kind of state.

Two things the system does not do yet. A lamp shows activity, but there is no “waiting for you” state. And agents do not pass work to each other through the world. Any pipeline that runs from place to place is the user’s own scripts and agent instructions.

Real · live stream, 30 Oct 2026A Hermes session on a wall terminal (right), with other agents’ screens across the room. Cropped still; face camera, stream label and game HUD removed.

## 04What we’ve seen so far

Everything here comes from Harrison using Omo Space as his main workspace for five days, live on stream, 25–29 October 2026: about 29 hours of transcribed streams. He ran a real content pipeline (ideas, references, recording, editing, publishing, analytics) with roughly one agent per stage. A friend also built his own world with it and showed it on stream.

We saw place used in four ways: to find, to resume, to monitor and to orchestrate. The quotes are what was said on stream. They are reports, not measurements.

### By the numbers

These come from Hermes’ own token counters, not from memory. Across all of Harrison’s agent profiles:

Day (AEDT)TokensModel callsAgent profiles

Sat 25 Oct0.09 bn9703

Sun 26 Oct0.63 bn5,0049

Mon 27 Oct0.56 bn3,9899

Tue 28 Oct4.17 bn25,38611

Wed 29 Oct1.61 bn7,80812

Five days7.07 bn43,157

Thu 30 Oct4.67 bn21,05020

That is about 7 billion tokens in five days, and over 4 billion on 28 October alone. Most of it (96%) is long agent conversations being re-read from the prompt cache on every step; new output was about half a percent. At list prices Hermes estimates the five days at about $3,400 (an estimate, not a bill). The counters include all of his Hermes work, not only work done through the world.

### Find: walk to it

Every workspace sits in a fixed, named place. You remember where an agent is, not which tab it was in. Live on the first night, Harrison named the problem the world was built to fix:

“Getting lost with all these tabs and things” [T1, 01:13:45, live]

Later he reported about 25 sessions running at once, “within the interface that we can conceptually understand” [T6, 07:37:22, live].

Real · live stream, 30 Oct 2026Find: a corridor of places, each with its own screen. The image shows layout, not an outcome.

### Resume: come back to it

The agents run outside the game, so leaving the game does not stop them, and the place is still there when you return. After quitting and reloading on the first night:

“So we can close it enjoy our day And then Come back Boom the agents are still working right here” [T1, 02:12:55, live]

On 29 October he said agents had kept editing, about 22 clips, after he closed Minecraft [T8, 00:06:30–00:08:38, live]. That fits the table above: closing the game does not stop jobs. It does not mean work ran while the PC was off; a restart stops running jobs. He also tied this to how it felt to start work: “I’m not dreading any pain / Or like context loss because I know anytime I want to work on the robotics project / I just fly down here” [T4, 02:21:42, live].

### Monitor: glance at lit screens

Lamps and lit screens let you read activity from across a room. The friend described exactly this cue, live, in his own world:

“How I can tell when the task is like running because their screen will turn on” [T8, 00:48:43, live; a friend, speaker inferred]

He also said watching the team was more fun than “just looking at you know Claude you know just typing” [T8, 01:00:57, live; a friend, speaker inferred].

Lamps show who is busy. They do not yet show that an agent is waiting for an answer; that is the next signal to build.

Real · live stream, 30 Oct 2026Monitor: lit screens readable from the cavern entrance. The image shows layout, not an outcome.

### Orchestrate: move work room to room

Harrison laid his content pipeline out as a row of places, about one stage and one agent each:

“We just go to that room and just start building / And when we’re done, then we just leave that room” [T2, 01:04:14, live]

By 29 October he wanted a place for each to-do item, “a repeatable pattern” [T8, 03:28:22, live].

The hand-offs between rooms are his own scripts and agent instructions. Laying the pipeline out in space made its stages visible and easy to visit.

### Places at every scale

The places were not just rooms. The pipeline lived in a cave of five rooms. He wanted whole worlds for lines of work: “We can build a whole world for the paid ads” [T7, 02:48:38, live]. To show how personal it could get, he imagined a pirate ship holding your tax work; that one stayed an idea. He said agents did most of the building: “I didn’t build any of this” [T6, 07:45:10, live].

Real · live stream, 30 Oct 2026An atrium.

Real · live stream, 30 Oct 2026A hall, with an embodied agent.

A friend took the idea his own way. New to Hermes and on Windows, he described about 24 hours of work: “It just gave Claude the GitHub and then gave it a few prompts and then it just it built the world” [T8, 01:04:44, live; a friend, speaker inferred]. His world had an AI office with a manager agent, teams, a podium and a sports arena; those were his own additions, not part of Omo Space.

## 05Web pages with a terminal attached

Late in the week Harrison described the core pattern in its most general form, apart from Minecraft:

“the concept of spatial interfaces with persistent webpages is easy to use and talk to and control. … We’re doing it inside Minecraft, but I believe there is not enough … attention, these persistent webpages with a terminal attached to it. And with this, you can build whatever pipeline that you want.” [T8, 03:38:57–03:39:18, live]

Pieced together from several moments, the pattern goes like this. You ask an agent at a station for a page for one job: a review queue, an analytics view, a publishing form. You pin it on a wall in the right place. You check it, and you approve or ask for changes through the terminal next to it. Then you come back to it later.

The page does the job-specific work. The place gives it a fixed home next to related work. The terminal beside it means the page is never finished; you can always ask the agent to change it. An ordinary browser tab could host the same page, and we have not separated those two effects. The in-world browser has limits too: drop-down menus could not be selected [T8, 03:22:45, live].

Real · live stream, 30 Oct 2026A page with a terminal attached: the review stage of the video pipeline, with approve, send back and move-to-done controls, beside the editing agent’s terminal.

## 06Design lessons

- Give work a place. A persistent, recognisable place per line of work, with room for several sessions per place, mirrored screens and any scale.

- Separate address from state. A place is an address. The process, the conversation, the page and the world behind it each need their own stated guarantee, and each needs testing.

- Activity is not “waiting for you”. A lit screen says busy. A question needs its own state, and a signal that follows the person into other rooms. Do not rely on colour alone.

- Make hand-offs explicit. Moving work between places should be a visible object or action, not something implied by layout.

- Let the work choose the shape. Rooms, caves, towers, ships, whole worlds; built by agents or by hand.

- Honest state. Never show progress that is not happening. Re-run nothing on the user’s behalf. Make the cost of the world itself visible, not only the work it saves.

## 07What’s next

We do not claim worlds beat tabs. We have not measured that. Here is what we’d like to measure next.

- Finding. How fast can someone find a named agent among 12 or 24 sessions in a world, compared with tabs? The tab side should be fair: same agents, same persistence, good names, status badges and search, so any difference comes from space and not from better tools.

- Resuming. After a day away, how long until the first useful action, in a world versus tabs?

- A “waiting for you” signal. We have not built it yet. Once it exists: is a blocked agent noticed sooner? And does it still work when the agent is in another room, or only with a signal that follows you?

- One-prompt places. Logging every place an agent builds, including failed and abandoned ones, to see how many get used as-is, how many need fixing, and how many are still in use two weeks later.

Some of the raw material already exists: bridge logs of sleep, resume and interruption events, the Hermes session stores, and the recordings.

## 08Prior work

Using space to organise computer work is an old idea. Rooms (1986) split a crowded screen into virtual rooms [2]. Data Mountain (1998) showed people can use spatial memory to place and find documents [3]. The Task Gallery (2000) hung running applications on the walls of a 3D gallery [4]. Calm technology argued for displays that show state “without being obtrusive” [5]. All of that was about documents, windows and tasks, not agents that keep working on their own. The closest recent work tackles agent supervision with dashboards: ParallelPilot adds “an ambient dashboard alongside existing coding tools” [6], and AgentGUI is an interface for observing and steering long-running agents [7]. Both report controlled user experiments; we have none. What Omo Space adds is a combination: places, built by people or by agents, that hold long-running sessions and agent-made pages.

- G. Robertson, M. Czerwinski, K. Larson, D. Robbins, D. Thiel and M. van Dantzich. 1998. Data Mountain: Using spatial memory for document management. In Proc. UIST ’98. ACM. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/data-mountain-using-spatial-memory-for-document-management

- G. Robertson et al. 2000. The Task Gallery: A 3D window manager. In Proc. CHI ’00. ACM. https://doi.org/10.1145/332040.332482
