## —About this paper

These are findings from the author’s own use of a system he built, not a controlled study. One person used it as his main workspace, live on stream, and a friend built his own world with it. There is no comparison with tabs and nothing was measured. The longer research paper, Worlds, Not Windows (working paper, draft v1.8), has the full method, episodes and limitations.

Quotes come from the stream transcripts, which were made automatically (Whisper) and may contain errors. Transcripts have no speaker labels; where a quote is from the friend, the speaker is inferred from context. Locators such as [T1, 02:12:55] name the transcript segment and time; every quoted span was checked by script against that transcript. Live means said while working.

Images are labelled by source. Real · live stream images are cropped stills from the author’s stream of 30 October 2026, the day after the period described, with real agent sessions; they show what the places look like, not outcomes. The one Illustration is generated and is not a screenshot.

---

# Bodies in the Block World: Robots Inside Minecraft

URL: https://www.omo.sh/research/robots

Working paper from Omo Research: a simulated Microduck, an RP1 humanoid, a ceiling AI and an agent player in one Minecraft world. What worked and what broke.

Abstract

Omo Space puts AI agents at desks inside Minecraft. Each desk is a terminal, and the agent in it does not move. Over three days in late October 2026 we tried giving agents bodies. We built four. Two are open-source robots simulated in MuJoCo and drawn in the game: Pollen Robotics' Microduck and RoboParty's RP1 humanoid. The third is a GLaDOS-style ceiling AI, a hanging chain of joints moved by scripted behaviour on top of physics. The fourth is OMO, a Mineflayer bot that joins the world as a player and is driven by a Hermes agent with 22 tools. The robots share one pattern: a local process owns the body, a client mod draws it, and a voice backend speaks for it. You talk to the body you are near or looking at. This paper describes the systems, lists what happened in order, and says plainly what broke.

01

## Introduction

1Terminaltext in a window

→

2Wallthe terminal, pinned to a place

3Avataran agent that is a player

4Simulated robota real design, physics and a policy

Omo Space started from one idea: a place is easier to remember than a tab. An agent gets a desk in a room, its terminal hangs on the wall, and you walk to it. The public guide states the limit: "A Hermes desk agent does not act in the world. It cannot walk, place blocks or press buttons." S10

That limit raises a question. If the world is the interface, should the agents in it have bodies? What does a body add that a wall does not?

We think of it as a ladder of embodiment:

- Terminal. The agent is text in a window.

- Wall. The same terminal, pinned to a place in a shared world. You find it by walking.

- Avatar. The agent is a player. It can walk to you, follow you, carry things and fight.

- Simulated robot. The body is a real robot design, moved by a physics engine and a trained policy, not by an animation.

Omo Space already had the first two rungs. This paper is about the last two. We did not set out to test the ladder. We built one body, it worked well enough to show, and then we built three more. The questions came after. They are in Section 7.

Two caveats. The evidence is one builder's streams, logs and repositories, plus a few friends and viewers who joined in. Nothing was compared against a control. And most of the code was written by coding agents from short prompts typed inside the game: "I just asked Opus55 bring RoboDuck into Minecraft." (T5 02:10:03) S12

02

## Background

Agents in Minecraft. Minecraft is a common testbed for language-model agents. Voyager calls itself "the first LLM-powered embodied lifelong learning agent in Minecraft", built on an automatic curriculum and a skill library of code S1. MINDcraft is "an easily extensible platform built to enable LLM agents to control characters in the open-world game of Minecraft" S2. OMO's body uses Mindcraft's skill library S3 on Mineflayer, which offers a "high level JavaScript API" for Minecraft bots S4.

Physics and robots. MuJoCo is a physics engine for model-based control S5. Pollen Robotics publishes the Microduck's MJCF model and meshes S6 and pretrained ONNX policies S7. Community members have published more Microduck policies on Hugging Face. RoboParty publishes the RP1's description files S8 and deploy code with pretrained policies S9.

We did not find prior work that puts a real robot design into the same game world as the people and the desk agents, where you walk up to it and talk. We did not search hard, so treat that as weak.

03

## Systems

The three robot bodies share one design, written down first for the duck. The RP1 and GLaDOS contracts say to read the duck's files and "copy freely" S13S16.

- A sidecar: one Python process that steps the simulation in real time and serves poses over HTTP on 127.0.0.1 only, "never 0.0.0.0" S13.

- A client mod for Minecraft 26.2 (Fabric). It fetches the mesh once, polls poses at about 25 Hz on a background thread, and draws each part every frame, smoothed between poses. Chat commands (!duck, !rp1, !glados) are caught on the client and never reach the server.

- An optional voice backend. A Simple Voice Chat plugin sends push-to-talk audio to it and plays the reply from the body's head, as positional sound, with captions.

Sidecars run on one thread at low priority, "so it never steals CPU from the game/OBS" S13. The builder plays and streams on the same machine.

### 3.1 Microduck

From the gameFive Microducks in the lab, each with its own eye colour and persona

Sim renderThe duck model the game draws, rendered in MuJoCo

Body. Pollen Robotics' Microduck, about 25 cm tall, with its real CAD, servo model and policies. MuJoCo runs at 200 Hz physics and 50 Hz policy, with the BAM XL330 servo model and 2° gear backlash S11. Each step builds the 61-number observation the policies were trained on S12a. Pollen's velstand policy walks, turns, follows and gets up; alpha_sitstand sits and stands S14. A duck still down after 3 s is reset upright S12a.

Blocks as terrain. Every 2 s the mod scans the blocks near the duck and sends their collision boxes to the sim. Walls stop it, carpets are walkable, ledges drop it. At the default scale a block is 25 cm, the duck's own height, so it cannot climb stairs. The README calls that "physically correct" S11.

A flock. Up to 4 ducks by default, 8 at most, each with a persona, name tag, eye colour and quack pitch: Quackers, Rusty, Zippy, Plato and Newton S11. Each duck has its own MuJoCo model, and the others appear in it as trunk-sized capsules S12a.

More brains. Twelve community policies are offered: sprint, roller skates, forward roll, cartwheel, hop, dance and others. Each was graded in the sim over 3 seeds first. Some were rejected, such as sprinters that "ignore the speed command, so nothing can stop them at the leash" S12a.

Cost. About 7% of one core for one duck and 22% for four, at a steady 50.0 Hz with 0 overruns, and about 470 MB of RAM. The model has 25,536 triangles S11.

Voice. Hold push-to-talk within 16 blocks. The backend picks the listener in this order: a duck named in your words, then the duck you just spoke to (for 20 s), then the duck under your crosshair, then the nearest, then the default S12b. Each duck has its own voice call, at most 2 open at once. Spoken moves are parsed locally into sidecar commands, with no agent round trip; other requests can go to a Hermes agent S20. The public release ships the voice plugin and protocol, not the backend. Stream viewers can walk the duck but cannot reset or remove it S11.

### 3.2 RP1 humanoid

Stream clipThe RP1 humanoid next to a Microduck in the underground lab

Body. RoboParty's RP1, 24-joint variant, with RoboParty's own policies: locomotion, a wave learned from a motion clip, and a dance S15. MuJoCo steps at 0.002 s with a 50 Hz policy. Joint PD control uses the gains from RoboParty's training setup. The hardware gains were tried first; with them the robot stood and turned but did "not walk forward (0.0 m/s at cmd 0.4)" S15.

Measured. Walking 0.395 m/s with 4 cm of sideways drift over 10 s. Turns of +86° and −85° in 2.6 s. Two 10-minute runs of random commands: 0 falls, 0 resets. CPU 8.1% of one core standing, 15.5% dancing S15.

In the world. One sim metre is one block, so RP1 stands about 1.5 blocks tall S17. Unlike the duck, "the robot can't see Minecraft blocks" S15. There is no get-up policy, so every fall ends in a reset.

Voice. A persona called Roboto, with his own voice. While he talks, a small waist sway and forearm movement are added to the standing policy, and only while he stands S15S20.

### 3.3 GLaDOS-style ceiling AI

Body. A large AI hanging from the lab ceiling, about 7.5 blocks tall, in the style of the Portal games. The first model was original procedural geometry with "no Valve assets". Two credited fan-made models were added later; the model switches live in about 0.1 s S16.

Physics without a policy. No trained policy exists for a character like this, so "the 'brain' is a scripted behaviour layer on top of real physics" S16. She is a chain of 13 hinge joints under gravity at 60 Hz. Gravity compensation on the arm is cut to 50%, so it "still hangs like a pendulum and sways from the reaction torques of the head". Inverse kinematics keeps her eye on the player. Behaviours include track, angry, scan, bow, sleep, dance and an 18.6 s "spooky" routine that ends with her eye about 1.5 m from the player's. Tracking error was 0.8–4.7° over 8 targets; the service used 5.6% of one core S16.

Voice. Her persona is written in our own words: a dry lab supervisor who calls the player "test subject" S16. One version re-voices her lines through a local voice-cloning speech server S20.

One listener at a time. Three companions in one room means three possible listeners. Each claims the mic when you are within range and looking at it, or closer to it than to the duck. The best fresh claim wins, so "exactly one companion hears each push-to-talk" S17.

### 3.4 OMO, the agent player

From the gameOMO, the agent player, in the cave base

Body. Not a simulated robot. OMO is a Mineflayer bot that logs into your single-player world as a player. He walks, swims, takes knockback, gets hungry, fights and sleeps S18. Omo Space v1.2.0 opens the world to LAN on port 25566 for agents on the same computer; offline logins from other machines are refused. Agents get the Omo skin and a ChatGPT - <name> tag S10bS18.

Brain and tools. You talk to a voice model in a browser page. Requests to do something go to OMO's own Hermes agent, which plans and calls the body's 22 tools over MCP. Long jobs can be interrupted, paused for a fight and resumed. "Come here", "follow me", "stop", "fight" and "chop some wood" skip the language model entirely S18S19.

What this rung adds. The robots move and talk. OMO changes the world. On stream he went from wood to planks, sticks, a crafting table and a pickaxe, then stone and a stone sword, "including retrying a craft that failed the first time" S18.

04

## What we did

Times are Australian Eastern Daylight Time, from commits, file times and CHANGELOGs. Stream tags (T4 = 27 Oct, T5–T7 = 28 Oct, T8 = 29 Oct) are offsets into each recording, not clock times S21.

27 October. - Around midday, four commits to the Omo Space mod opened single-player worlds to local agents over LAN, let a plain bot client join a Fabric world, and added the agent skin and name tag S22. - On stream, OMO appeared carrying a sword and following the builder (T4 00:12:59). Asked to use Hermes to find a bot's-eye camera plugin, he came back with "prismarine viewer" (T4 02:39:45) S21. - A viewer had suggested putting the Microduck in Minecraft: "you were the one that gave me the idea" (T4 02:17:24). One prompt to a desk agent built an underground robotics lab, shown about 30 minutes later (T4 02:52:47). The duck was reported built and installed at T4 03:27:36 S21.

28 October, night to morning. - The duck walked on command in the game (T5 00:11:45). The RP1 was spawned and danced (T5 00:55:46): "Now it's truly online." (T5 00:56:30) S21 - First push-to-talk conversation with the duck (T5 01:35:42). "Microduck? Do a jump." worked (T5 01:44:29) S21. - The GLaDOS project began from the same pattern (T5 01:55:23) S21. Her sidecar got a redesign, then switchable fan-made models (live from about 06:31), then the spooky routine S16S23. - Multi-duck support began around 03:30 (a backup folder marks it) S12a. Soon after: "Yo ducks ducks race to my position" (T5 03:02:26) S21.

28 October, day. - 12:28: Omo Microduck v1.0.0, the first public release S24. 14:26: Omo, brought to life v0.1.0 S25. - On stream, six ducks stood up and walked toward the builder (T6 06:51:55). Ducks answered spoken commands in character ("Quack. We're doing it.", T7 03:20:52), and agents cut stream clips of them into short films S21.

29 October. The builder spoke to the flock in passing: "can two of the ducks sit down and the rest stand up" (T8 01:47:37) S21.

30 October. The RP1 and GLaDOS code went into local version control, "not published" S26.

05

## Observations

From the gameA Microduck mid forward roll, one of the community policies

These are things we saw, not things we tested.

A real robot design reads differently from a mob. The duck falls because a policy lost its balance against simulated gravity, not because an animation played. Its stair falls became a public reel: "It can't climb stairs, so down it goes" S11. The failure was the content.

Proximity and gaze worked as addressing. Push-to-talk "within our 16 blocks" (T5 01:20:59), with the crosshair or a name choosing the listener, was enough to talk to one duck in a flock. "Each microduck will have its own personality." (T5 01:46:32) S21. The question from the same stream is still open: "How does it know where I'm talking to?" (T5 03:03:09) S21a.

Other people joined in. Friends on a call directed the robots ("Scale like five or six.", T5 02:19:50). One asked whether the robots could do real work, "like hold something", or were "just regular robots" (T6 07:52:13) S21. That question marks the gap between the robot rung and the avatar rung.

The game became the lab. The robots got a test room, an obstacle course and a separate dev room. One line on a call was "This is the simulator." (T5 02:15:53); the speaker is uncertain S21.

Only the avatar does work. OMO answered two overlapping spoken requests in one reply, a web lookup and his inventory ("four pieces of rotten flesh") S18. The robots never change the world. OMO does.

06

## What broke, and limitations

Stream reelThe duck meets Minecraft stairs: a fall from the stream, as posted

Speed of building, and its cost. Each new body reused the duck's design and took hours, not days S15S17. We cannot tell how much of that was the pattern and how much was the coding agents.

Physics meets blocks. The duck fell on stairs again and again ("The micro doc is just forming on our Minecraft stairs.", T5 01:34:03) and got stuck (T8 03:32:15). Early on it walked through walls (T5 00:11:58), before terrain was added. The RP1 still cannot see blocks and walked through walls in a demo (T6 07:57:55) S15S21.

Sim gaps. The duck's walking policy reaches about ⅓ of its commanded speed in our CPU sim, so commands are scaled and speeds are "nominal" S11. The RP1 reaches about 0.8× S15. Ducks feel each other only as capsules S12a.

The humanoid would not follow. "rp1 follow me and it's not working but maybe the ducks" (T6 07:56:20) S21. The cause is [unverified].

Voice. The cloned GLaDOS voice ran slower than real time: "I'm rating 9.2 seconds of speech. / Took 15 seconds." (T6 04:45:58), and later "So, she is broken." (T6 05:17:38) S21. OMO's voice runs in a browser tab, not in-game push-to-talk, over an undocumented route that "can change or break without notice" S18.

The agent player is fragile. He would not stay put ("Stay sit sit puppy sit right not working", T4 00:13:26). He talked over the builder (T4 02:49:11). He kept dying to zombies, and the builder worried it was "using up my usage" (T4 03:04:49). One Hermes round trip never came back (T4 03:35:07) S21. A request for 8 birch logs ended with 1 S18.

The machine. The 28 October stream ends in a full PC freeze and restart S21.

Opacity. Asked how the duck was connected, the builder said "I don't even know bro." (T5 02:10:02) S21. Building by prompt is fast. It can also leave the builder unable to debug live.

Rights. The Microduck mod and the agent player are public under MIT, with upstream credits S11S18. The RP1 work is "local personal use only" S15. The GLaDOS work uses a character owned by Valve, fan-made models credited for personal non-commercial use, and a cloned character voice S16S20. It is not published, and should not be.

Evidence. One builder, a few friends and viewers. Quotes come from automatic transcripts, checked against the transcript text but not the audio S21.

07

## Next steps and testable questions

- Addressing. With 3 or more companions in a room, how often does a spoken request reach the intended listener? Compare routing by name, gaze and nearness. The routing is already logged S20.

- Trust. Does a body that can really fall make people more or less willing to hand an agent a real task than a scripted one does?

- Robots that work. Connect a simulated robot to a Hermes agent with real tools, as OMO is connected. Can it "hold something"?

- Terrain for the humanoid. Port the duck's block scan to the RP1. Measure falls per minute on a fixed obstacle course, before and after.

- Getting up. Add a get-up policy for the RP1 and count resets per 10 minutes.

- Long chains. Run OMO's stone-sword chain 20 times from a fresh world. How often does it finish, and why does it fail?

- Cost. Measure game frame time with 0, 1, 4 and 8 bodies loaded, on the streaming machine, while streaming.

08

# Omo R1: An AI Agent Player in Your Minecraft World

URL: https://www.omo.sh/research/omo-r1

Omo R1 joins your Minecraft world as a real player. Talk to him out loud; a Hermes agent plans the job and his body does it with 22 tools. Open source, MIT.

Abstract

Omo R1 is our first agent brought all the way to life in Minecraft. He is not a chatbot in a side window. He logs into your single-player world as a real player, you talk to him out loud, he answers in his own voice, and then he goes and does it S1. Three parts make him: a realtime voice model that listens and speaks, a Hermes agent that plans, and a Mineflayer body that serves 22 tools to that agent S1S2. He was released as open source on 28 October 2026, after a first live run on stream the day before S3. This page describes how he works, what he did on stream, and where he still falls short.

01

## Introduction

The desk agents in Omo Space work in terminals. They cannot walk, place blocks or press buttons S4. That keeps them safe and simple, but it also means the world around them is scenery.

From our streamOmo R1 in the underground base, 27 October

Omo R1 is the next step on our ladder of embodiment: from a terminal, to a terminal on a wall, to an agent that is a player S5. At Omo Research we want agents that are present: with a body, a place and a voice S1. R1 is the first one that has all three.

02

## What he is

From our streamHe follows you through the base on his own legs

From our streamA player entity with a body, a skin and a name tag

- A body. Omo logs into your world as a player called ChatGPT - OMO, with his own skin. He walks, jumps, swims, takes knockback, gets hungry, fights and sleeps. Other mobs see him as a player, because he is one S1.

- A place. He lives where you play. He sees the blocks, mobs and players around him, carries an inventory, and uses the same crafting tables, furnaces and chests that you do S1.

- A voice. You press "Start talking" and speak. A realtime voice model listens and answers, full duplex, in Omo's own voice, a warm old grandad. When you ask for something real, a Hermes agent plans it and drives his body S1S3.

03

## How it works

- Voice. A local web page opens a realtime voice call. The voice model chats on its own; when you ask Omo to do something, it hands the request off as a delegation S1S2.

- Brain. Each delegation goes to Omo's own Hermes profile. Hermes plans with the omo-body skill and calls body tools until the job is done. Requests that arrive mid-job are queued, and every answer goes back to the newest request, so the voice always says it S1.

- Body. A Mineflayer bot named OMO joins your world over LAN and serves its actions as an MCP server. Its skills are Mindcraft's library, wrapped in jobs that can be interrupted, paused for a fight and resumed S1S6S7.

- World. Omo Space v1.2.0 opens your single-player world to LAN for agents on the same computer only, lets a plain bot client join, and gives agents the Omo skin and name tag S1S4.

Short, plain requests such as "come here", "follow me", "stop", "fight" and "chop some wood" take a fast path straight to the body, so they never wait on a language model S1S2.

04

## What he can do

His body serves 22 tools to Hermes. Each returns a short fact he can say out loud S1:

Group Tools

See where he is, health, food, nearby players, blocks and mobs, inventory; what he can craft now

Move come to you, follow you, stop, go to coordinates, go to the nearest block of a type, look at you

Fight guard mode (on by default), attack the nearest monster, hunt a mob type

Work chop and mine with the right tool, craft, smelt, place blocks, use chests, pick up and give items, equip tools and armour

Live eat, sleep in the nearest bed, type in chat

He also has reflexes he uses without being asked: he fights back, backs off and eats when his health is low, gets out of lava, fire and deep water, wears the best armour he picks up, and looks at whoever hits him S1.

05

## What he did on stream

On the 27 October 2026 live stream, from the bridge log S1:

From our streamWaiting by the rooms of the base while a job runs

- A whole crafting chain. "Make me a stone sword" became: collect wood, craft planks, sticks, a crafting table and a wooden pickaxe, mine stone, craft the sword, equip it. He ran the whole chain himself, "including retrying a craft that failed the first time" S1.

- Following through the base. He followed the builder through the underground base and up the stairs, on his own legs S1.

- Two requests at once. Asked to look something up and, at the same time, what was in his inventory, he answered both in one reply: "I've got four pieces of rotten flesh and nothing else. Not exactly a gourmet picnic." S1

Because his brain is a full Hermes agent, he can also do real work outside the world when asked: look something up, read a file, check a project S1.

06

## Verified

The v0.1.0 release ships with 18 tests, all passing on Linux x86_64 with Node 22 S1S3:

Suite What it covers Result

Voice sessions, delegation parsing, newest-delegation delivery and queueing 7/7

Body the LAN file, MCP tools, follow, fast-path movement and combat, jobs pausing for a fight and resuming 8/8

Hygiene no tokens or machine paths in the tree; the README's tools table matches the served tools 3/3

07

## Limitations

- Jobs can come up short. On stream, a request for 8 birch logs finished with 1 collected. He reports the real count, so Hermes has to notice and retry. Long gather-then-craft chains are the weakest part today S1.

- The voice route is not a public API. It uses your own ChatGPT login against the endpoint the Codex app uses. It can change or break without notice, and usage counts against your subscription S1.

- You talk through a browser tab. In-game push-to-talk is not wired up for Omo yet S1.

- Minecraft 26.2 is newer than released Mineflayer. Installing patches in 26.2 data, and multi-item crafts desync, so he crafts one batch at a time S1.

- He is slow to think. Hermes replies take 8 to 12 seconds in the log, so the voice says "on it" first S1.

- He is one agent, for one player. Use it for yourself; do not run it as a service for others S1.

08

## Next

The questions we want to answer next are in our robots paper: how often a long chain like the stone sword finishes from a fresh world, and why it fails when it doesn't S5. We also want him to hear you through in-game push-to-talk, the way our robot ducks already do S5.

09

## Sources

[S1] Omo, brought to life: README (public). github.com/omoresearch/omo-brought-to-life. "Not a chatbot in a side window. Omo is a player in your Minecraft world"

[S2] Omo, brought to life: How it works (public). github.com/omoresearch/omo-brought-to-life/blob/main/docs/how-it-works.md. "runs them on the body directly, before any language model."

[S3] Omo, brought to life: CHANGELOG, v0.1.0 "First breath", 28 October 2026 (public). github.com/omoresearch/omo-brought-to-life/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md. "The first public release of Omo as one repo: voice, brain, body and the mod changes that let him in."

[S4] Omo Space docs, Agents and terminals (public). github.com/omoresearch/omo-space/blob/main/docs/AGENTS-AND-TERMINALS.md. "A Hermes desk agent does not act in the world. It cannot walk, place blocks or press buttons."

[S5] Bodies in the Block World. Omo Research working paper, October 2026. www.omo.sh/research/robots/

[S6] Mindcraft. github.com/mindcraft-bots/mindcraft

[S7] Mineflayer. github.com/PrismarineJS/mineflayer

Not an official Minecraft product. Not approved by or associated with Mojang or Microsoft. Not affiliated with or endorsed by OpenAI. Body skills are Mindcraft's library on Mineflayer (MIT); the brain is Hermes Agent by Nous Research.

# What Is a Spatial AI Agent? A Working Definition

URL: https://www.omo.sh/notes/what-is-a-spatial-ai-agent

A practical definition of a spatial AI agent: an agent that perceives place, builds spatial memory, acts in an environment, and makes its presence understandable.

01 / Definition

## Spatial agency begins when place changes what the agent can know and do

Our working definition: a spatial AI agent is a software system whose perception, memory, decisions, or actions are meaningfully organized by relationships in a physical or virtual environment—and whose situated behavior can be understood and redirected by people.

The first half connects spatial agency to embodied AI. AI Habitat describes embodied AI in terms of intelligent machines with a physical or virtual embodiment and studies tasks such as navigation, instruction following, and question answering. The second half adds an interface requirement. A capable system is not automatically a good collaborator. People need cues about where it is, what it can perceive, why it moved, and how to intervene.

“Spatial” therefore means more than rendering an avatar beside a chat box. Position must have consequences. Distance might change what is audible or relevant. Orientation might determine what is perceived. A room might hold persistent context. Movement might be an action, a signal, or both.

02 / Four layers

## A practical stack for spatial agency

01

### Situated perception

The agent receives observations from somewhere: a camera view, coordinates, nearby objects, sound direction, or a bounded field of attention. It cannot treat all context as equally present.

02

### Spatial memory

The agent retains useful relations among places, objects, people, and prior events. It can distinguish “beside,” “behind,” “where we met,” and “the route that failed.”

03

### Situated action

The agent can alter its position or the environment: navigate, point, place, retrieve, open, build, or hand off. Action is constrained by reach, access, time, and other occupants.

04

### Social legibility

The system communicates attention, intention, uncertainty, and availability in ways a nearby person can interpret. Presence becomes part of the interface contract.

Research platforms make the technical layers concrete. Habitat Lab lets researchers define agents with physical forms, sensors, capabilities, and tasks. Project Malmo exposes sensing and acting inside Minecraft. Neither project implies Omo’s social-legibility layer; that layer is our design proposal for turning spatial intelligence into a human-facing interface.

03 / Boundaries

## What does not count on its own

Not sufficient

A 3D avatar

Representation is not agency. If place never changes perception, memory, or action, the space is decoration.

A map lookup

A system can answer geographic questions without occupying a position or maintaining a situated relationship to a world.

A remote cursor

Moving a pointer can act on a screen, but it does not by itself create spatial memory, constraints, or presence.

These can still be ingredients. An avatar can signal gaze. A map can support route planning. A cursor can reveal intent. The distinction is whether spatial relationships participate in the loop from observation to memory to choice to action—and whether a human can read that loop well enough to coordinate with it.

04 / Design questions

## The questions a spatial interface should answer without a manual

### Where is the agent’s attention?

A person should be able to tell what the system is attending to, and distinguish looking from knowing.

### What will happen if I move?

Proximity and orientation need consistent meaning. Crossing a boundary should not silently change permissions or context.

### What does this place remember?

Persistent context needs visible scope, ownership, and expiry. A room that remembers is also a room that can surprise.

### How do I stop or correct it?

Intervention must work at the pace of action. A spatial agent should make pausing, redirecting, and undoing easier than watching.

This shifts evaluation from abstract intelligence toward lived coordination. Did the agent reach the destination? Did the person understand its route? Could they predict its next action? Did the space clarify responsibility or obscure it? The strongest spatial system may not be the most autonomous one. It may be the one that makes joint action easiest.

05 / Primary sources

## Foundations for the definition

### AI Habitat — embodied AI platform ↗

A simulation platform and research community for intelligent machines with physical or virtual embodiment.

### Habitat Lab documentation ↗

Defines tasks, agents, sensors, capabilities, training approaches, and benchmark metrics for embodied AI.

### Project Malmo — Microsoft Research ↗

A Minecraft-based platform that lets agents sense and act in complex, varied environments.

06 / Continue

## See the definition inside a world

Related Omo Note

Minecraft makes spatial agency inspectable.

The related note looks at a shared game world as interface material for visible action, collaboration, recovery, and persistent traces.

Read the Minecraft note →Next: voice presence

# Minecraft as an Interface for AI Agents

URL: https://www.omo.sh/notes/minecraft-as-an-agent-interface

Why Minecraft is a useful interface and test world for AI agents: shared space, visible action, persistent consequences, collaboration, and human legibility.

01 / Why a world?

## Agency becomes easier to see when it has somewhere to happen

Most AI interfaces hide the sequence between intention and result. A person asks; the system answers. Even when an agent calls tools, the experience often collapses perception, planning, action, and recovery into a progress spinner. Minecraft stretches those steps across a world. To fetch wood, an agent must locate a tree, travel, select a tool, act, retain the result, and adjust when the route or resource changes.

That is one reason Minecraft has repeatedly served as an AI environment. Microsoft’s Project Malmo exposes a Minecraft-based platform in which agents sense and act. MineDojo frames Minecraft as an open-ended setting for embodied-agent research. The Voyager paper uses it to study an LLM-powered agent that explores, builds a reusable skill library, and improves programs using environmental feedback.

These projects are not evidence for every claim one might make about “general” agents. They do show why the environment is useful: it combines long tasks, many possible actions, partial knowledge, persistent objects, and consequences that both a human and a machine can inspect.

02 / Interface model

## The world is not only a benchmark. It can be the interface.

Our working model separates four kinds of legibility.

01

### Perceptual legibility

Where is the agent looking? What is near enough to matter? A body with a position and orientation makes the limits of perception discussable.

02

### Procedural legibility

Walking, opening, mining, crafting, and building expose the route between a request and its completion. A mistake has a location and a moment.

03

### Social legibility

A person can approach, follow, interrupt, demonstrate, or work alongside the agent. Cooperation is expressed through shared activity, not only messages.

04

### Historical legibility

A path, chest, unfinished wall, or changed landscape can become a durable trace. The environment carries some of the interaction history.

The technical threshold for exploring this is lower than it once was. Mineflayer provides a high-level API for Minecraft bots with world queries, movement, inventory, crafting, building, and chat. That does not make a bot intelligent. It does make the boundary between high-level intent and world action concrete enough to inspect.

03 / Design tests

## What would make a Minecraft agent feel present?

Test 01

Point before prose

Can the agent orient toward a place or object before explaining it, so language and attention agree?

Test 02

Recover in public

When a route or plan fails, can the agent make the failure visible and choose a comprehensible alternative?

Test 03

Leave useful traces

Can its actions create landmarks, storage, signs, or paths that help the next collaboration?

The most interesting evaluation may not be “did it complete the task?” alone. A collaborator also needs to know whether the agent stayed oriented to the shared goal, whether its next move was predictable, and whether intervention was easy. Completion, legibility, and corrigibility should be measured separately.

Voice adds another layer. “Meet me by the bridge” is a spatial instruction whose meaning depends on shared landmarks. “Put that over there” combines speech, pointing, and context. Minecraft offers a bounded place to ask how an agent should resolve those references, acknowledge uncertainty, and negotiate a plan while both parties can see the same consequences.

04 / Limits

## Minecraft is a lens, not the world

A block world has clean rules, discrete items, and forgiving consequences. Homes, streets, workplaces, and bodies do not. Success in Minecraft does not establish safety, reliability, or usefulness elsewhere. The environment can also tempt designers to optimize for spectacle—long autonomous runs or impressive builds—when the human question is whether the agent can be understood and redirected.

The Omo thesis is narrower: a shared world is a promising interface material because it makes agency observable. Minecraft is valuable where it lets us examine presence, coordination, memory, and repair. If a simpler environment answers a question more honestly, the simpler environment should win.

05 / Primary sources

## Projects behind this note

### Project Malmo — Microsoft Research ↗

An AI experimentation platform built on Minecraft for sensing, acting, learning, and collaboration research.

### MineDojo — project site ↗

An open-ended embodied-agent framework and dataset built around Minecraft.

### Voyager — paper and authors ↗

An LLM-powered Minecraft agent organized around an automatic curriculum, executable skill library, and iterative program improvement.

### Mineflayer — PrismarineJS ↗

An open-source high-level API for Minecraft bots and world interaction.

06 / Continue

## From world to spatial agency

Related Omo Note

What makes an agent spatial?

A body in a world is only the beginning. The next note proposes a working definition built around place, spatial memory, situated action, and understandable presence.

Read the spatial agent note →All notes

# Voice-First AI Presence: Beyond a Realistic Voice

URL: https://www.omo.sh/notes/voice-first-ai-presence

Voice-first AI presence is a turn-taking design problem: latency, interruption, silence, attention, and repair matter more than a realistic synthetic voice alone.

01 / Presence

## Voice is not a skin for text

A text interface lets both parties pause without explanation. Speech is less forgiving. Every delay sounds like hesitation or absence. Talking over someone feels different from producing a long paragraph. A response that cannot be interrupted becomes a small captivity. When an agent speaks, timing becomes visible behavior.

Modern systems expose capabilities needed for a more conversational loop. OpenAI describes its Realtime API as direct speech-to-speech processing designed for low-latency interaction. Google’s Live API documentation exposes voice activity detection, interruption handling, turn-coverage settings, and non-blocking tool behavior. These are platform capabilities, not proof that a particular experience feels natural. They reveal the design surface.

Our thesis is that voice-first AI should be judged as a participant in turn-taking, not as a text model with audio output. The voice itself matters, but the social mechanics around it matter more.

02 / Five signals

## What makes a voice agent feel attentive?

01

### Arrival

The system acknowledges that it heard something quickly, without pretending it already understands. A small signal can separate attentive delay from dead air.

02

### Turn boundaries

The agent distinguishes a pause for thought from the end of a turn. It leaves room for continuation and does not seize the floor at every silence.

03

### Interruptibility

A person can cut in, correct a premise, or stop an action. The agent yields promptly and does not finish a cached speech buffer over them.

04

### Economy

Spoken answers are shaped for the ear. The agent gives the next useful piece, then checks whether more detail is wanted.

05

### Repair

When hearing or intent is uncertain, it asks a narrow question, states the uncertainty, and preserves the part of the conversation that remains valid.

Interruption is especially revealing. Google’s documentation notes that voice activity detection can cancel ongoing generation and that clients should discard buffered audio after interruption. This implementation detail becomes an experiential rule: the system must stop sounding as soon as it stops holding the floor. A delayed client can make an interruptible model feel stubborn.

03 / Silence & space

## Sometimes presence means not answering

A voice agent in a phone call is invited to treat nearly every utterance as addressed to it. An agent in a room, game, vehicle, or shared workspace faces a harder question: was that speech for the agent, for another person, or simply thinking aloud? Always answering turns presence into intrusion.

Proactivity features point toward this problem. Google documents a mode in which a live model can decide not to respond when input is irrelevant. But relevance is not only semantic. It can depend on wake cues, gaze, distance, role, the current activity, and the cost of interruption. This is where voice and spatial agency meet: who is near, what they face, and what place they occupy can help define whether the agent has the floor.

Silence should not be mysterious. The interface can signal “listening,” “not addressed,” “working,” or “uncertain” without speaking a sentence. Presence is not maximum output. It is the right level of availability for the moment.

State

Listening

Available, but not claiming every sound as a request.

Thinking

Holding the task while leaving the person free to interrupt.

Receding

Remaining reachable without competing for attention.

04 / Design tests

## Measure the conversation, not only the model

### Time to acknowledgement

How quickly does the person know their speech was received, separate from the time needed for a full answer?

### Time to yield

From the start of a human interruption, how long until audible output actually stops at the speaker?

### False turn rate

How often does the agent answer a pause, side conversation, or ambient utterance that was not a completed request?

### Repair cost

After a misunderstanding, how many words and turns are required to restore shared context and continue?

These measures sit across model, network, audio pipeline, interface, and context policy. That is precisely the point. A voice experience is the whole loop. Evaluating transcription accuracy or response quality in isolation misses the behaviors people encounter most directly.

A useful voice-first agent should feel easy to begin, easy to interrupt, and easy to leave. Naturalness is not mimicry. It is shared control over attention and time.

05 / Primary sources

## Capabilities behind this note

### OpenAI Realtime API announcement ↗

Describes direct speech-to-speech processing, lower latency, tool use, and production voice-agent capabilities.

### Gemini Live API capabilities ↗

Documents voice activity detection, interruption, turn coverage, proactive audio, and asynchronous function behavior.

### Gemini Live API best practices ↗

Connects audio chunking, client buffering, and interruption handling to low-latency live interaction.

06 / Continue

## Put the voice somewhere

Related Omo Note

Presence changes when an agent shares a world.

Minecraft offers a legible place to connect speech with gaze, movement, landmarks, action, and visible recovery.

Read the Minecraft note →All notes

# Thirteen Interfaces We Tried for Working with AI Agents

URL: https://www.omo.sh/notes/interfaces-we-tried

A field report from Omo Research: thirteen voice, screen, and world interfaces we built and used for working with AI agents, and what each one taught us.

01 / Approach

## Build it, use it for real work, notice what we return to

Each interface started from the same question: what is the most natural way for one person to work with a team of AI agents? We built the smallest version that could answer it, used it for actual projects, and kept notes on what felt natural, what broke, and which tools we quietly stopped opening. The experiments fall under the three questions on our research agenda: voice, screens, and space.

02 / Voice

## Can speaking replace typing?

01

Apr 2026Prototype

### Talk to anything

Point a phone at a mug or a mouse, tap it, and it wakes up with a face, a personality, and a voice you can talk back to. Built at a hackathon.

ScreenshotHackathon demo: everyday objects with faces and voices

What we sawTalking out loud felt natural as soon as the thing we talked to had a face and a place.

02

May 2026Open source

### Holographic co-founder

A voice-first hologram that draws live business charts in the air, with a command terminal and a small pixel office where the agent team works. Built in two and a half days and placed third at a hackathon.

DemoHologram demo, from the open-source repo (demo data)

What we sawGiving the agent a body and a place made it feel present, which pointed us toward worlds instead of windows.

03

Oct 2026Open source

### Voice control from the phone

Ask out loud what's new, hear a spoken catch-up, and post into a thread by voice. Later versions also show the messages on screen.

ScreenshotThe open-source voice app's landing page (example conversation)

What we sawMost spoken requests were catch-ups (“any updates?”, “what's new?”), not instructions. Reading every post back for confirmation felt slow, and a voice app and a text chat on top of the same agent drifted into giving different answers.

03 / Screens

## Can the right app make many agents manageable?

04

Sep 2026Tried

### Terminal workspace

One space per project and one tab per agent profile in a terminal multiplexer.

DiagramOne tab per agent, split panes per task

What we sawThe most fluid text setup we used. It broke down on small things, like copying text over a remote connection.

05

Sep 2026Kept as the message layer

### Chat server as HQ

One channel per agent with its reasoning and tool calls visible, plus an HQ channel that sends work out and relays results back.

DiagramA channel per agent; HQ sends work out and relays results back

What we sawSeeing reasoning in the open helped. Nested threads got confusing fast, and the app felt heavy for what we used.

06

Sep–Oct 2026Stalled

### One chat that runs everything

Talk to one agent in one thread; it delegates to the others and reports back.

DiagramOne thread in front, the agents hidden behind it

What we sawIt was hard to tell which agent was actually answering. For a while, it was still the default one.

07

Sep 2026App retired

### Kanban boards

A web board and a native app to watch agent tasks move across columns.

DiagramAgent tasks moving across columns

What we sawGood for status at a glance. A separate app for it didn't stick.

08

### Browser extension

A community-built extension we tried, not one of ours: the agent in a side panel next to the page it is working on.

DiagramThe agent in a side panel next to the page

What we sawHandy next to a single page, but one more place to look.

09

### Status dashboard

A small desktop app for logs, service health, and API costs: the agent system as a dashboard instead of a conversation.

DiagramLogs, services, jobs, and API costs at a glance

What we sawGood for health and costs. It said nothing about what the agents were working on.

10

Sep 2026Prototype

### Glass desktop app

A lightweight native app with the same channel and thread structure as the chat server: about 206 MB of memory against roughly 1 GB, and ready in a quarter of a second.

DiagramChannels and threads in a lightweight glass window

What we sawA lighter skin on the same structure. Replies were only tested against a mock backend.

04 / Space

## Can a place replace the menu?

11

Jun–Aug 2026Led to the next step

### Agents in a Minecraft world

Agents living in a shared Minecraft world instead of a chat window.

ImageAgents at their desks in a Minecraft build

What we sawGave us our working idea: the world is the interface.

12

Sep 2026Led to Omo Space

### Minecraft as the interface

A real terminal inside Minecraft, a pocket computer you can type into, and in-game monitors that show live web pages.

ScreenshotIn-game footage: a live web page on a Minecraft monitor

What we sawThe first version felt slightly laggy. Once typing in the world was instant, it became the interface we kept coming back to.

13

Oct 2026 – nowNow

### Omo Space

One room per project and screens that stay where you left them, which became Omo Space: real AI agents at their own desks inside Minecraft, each with its terminal on the wall.

ScreenshotOmo Space: agent terminals and a live board on the walls

What we sawWalking to an agent's desk is a fast way to know what it is doing. This is what we use every day.

05 / Patterns

## What kept showing up

Pattern 01

Every setup rebuilt rooms

Tabs per agent, channels per agent, spaces per project. Each text interface ended up drawing a map. A world gives you that map directly.

Pattern 02

Voice is for catching up

Spoken requests were mostly status questions. Detailed instructions still went through typing.

Pattern 03

Speed decides everything

A beautiful interface that lags gets abandoned. The in-world terminal only stuck once typing felt instant.

Pattern 04

One agent, one front door

Two interfaces on the same agent drifted apart in tone and answers. Shared state underneath matters more than the skin on top.

Pattern 05

Persistence builds trust

Screens and desks that stay where you left them made it easy to pick up where an agent was.

Pattern 06

Hidden routing hurts

The more an interface hid which agent was doing what, the harder it was to fix things when they went wrong.

06 / Limits

## One small team, one set of habits

These observations come from a small team using its own tools. We did not run controlled comparisons, and most numbers here are from our own setup. Some ideas stalled for practical reasons, such as a bug or a missing feature, rather than because the idea failed. Treat this as a map of what we tried, not as evidence that one interface is better for everyone.

07 / Continue

## Where it led

Experiment 13, ongoing

Omo Space

Real AI agents at their own desks inside Minecraft, each with its terminal on the wall. It is what we use every day now, and where the next experiments will happen.

See Omo Space ↗Read the Minecraft note

# Omo Enterprise: Agentic Interfaces for Organisations

URL: https://www.omo.sh/enterprise

Give every AI agent in your organisation a place: spatial interfaces where teams find, resume and monitor dozens of agents. Built on open-source Omo Space.

Enterprise · Agentic interfaces

# Give every agent in your organisation a place.

Your teams are starting to run agents by the dozen, for hours at a time, and nobody can see anyone else’s. A chat window was built for one person and one conversation. We design spaces where people can find any agent, see which one needs them, and pick up where they left off.

Request a conversationWatch the demo →GitHub ↗

21–25agent sessions running at once, at peak, for one person

22agent profiles in our studio, one per role

114workspaces on one machine, 62 of them live

791quotes checked against 29 hours of footage

Measured in our own studio, 25–29 October 2026, and reported in our working paper Rooms, Not Windows. One builder plus one second user; not a controlled study.

01 / The problem

## One agent fits in a chat window. Twelve do not.

Agentic work means many agents that keep running for hours. Each one gets a tab, and every tab looks the same. Past a dozen, people lose track of three simple things.

Which is which?Twelve identical tabs, and the names stop meaning anything.

Which is working?Checking means opening every tab, one by one, all day.

Which is waiting for you?The agent that asked a question an hour ago is still waiting, silently.

“Nobody remembers which of the 12 terminal tabs are doing what but you can remember space and rooms … It’s the oldest memory trick out there.”From our stream, 28 Oct 2026

02 / And it gets worse with teams

## More people does not mean more done. It often means less.

Agents were designed as one person talking to one assistant. Put fifty people in a team, each running ten agents, and you have five hundred conversations that only their owners can see. Adding people to that does not add up; the coordination cost grows faster than the work.

Invisible to everyone elseEach person’s agents live in their own tabs. Nobody else can see what is running, what is stuck or what is already done.

Handoffs happen in chatWork moves between people by pasting outputs into messages. Context is lost at every step, and agents start again from zero.

Waiting on the wrong personAn agent asks a question its owner will not see until tomorrow, while the colleague who could answer it sits next to them.

Duplicated workTwo people set agents on the same problem, because nothing shows that someone already has.

No shape to the workA new hire cannot see how the team actually runs. The process lives in people’s heads and private chat histories.

Managers fly blindThe only way to know where things stand is to ask around, which is the very interruption agents were meant to remove.

### A place is shared by default.

In a space, the agents are not hidden inside someone’s laptop; they are in rooms everyone can walk into. The floor shows the whole team’s work at once: which room belongs to which team, which agents are working, which one is waiting, and who it is waiting for.

- One room per team or stageThe structure of the work is the building. New people learn it by walking it.

- Status anyone can readA lamp outside a room tells the whole team that an agent needs someone, not just its owner.

- Handoffs by walking, not pastingWork moves to the next room with its context, the way it moves through our studio pipeline.

Honest status: today a workspace lives on the computer that opened it, and a friend on another PC gets a fresh copy. Shared spaces for whole teams are what our pilots are for.

03 / See it

## A real workspace, not a mock-up.

This is our own world, filmed tonight. Every room is a job, and every room was built by an agent from a short request. In daily use each terminal on a wall is a live agent session on the computer underneath.

The library: our launch-video and branding room, one agent desk per job. In-game footage, 30 Oct 2026, filmed on a copy of the world, so these screens show log text rather than live agents.

The Glass Tower An office floor around a glass box, with an agent inside.

Mountain Studio An eight-stage video pipeline, one zone per stage.

The Lantern Grove The calm centre, with research papers on the walls.

04 / Why a place

## Four chores that break in a chat window, and work in a room.

People remember places far better than tabs; interface research has shown it for forty years. A spatial interface turns the four hardest parts of running many agents into things people already do well. Each of these came up in nearly every part of our five-day study.

Find · 8 of 8

### Walk to it

Each agent has a desk, a name plate and a screen. You find it the way you find a colleague.

“How do you keep track of your agents? I just walk around”Stream, 28 Oct

Resume · 8 of 8

### Come back to it

The work stays on the wall where you left it, through closed screens, restarts and days away.

“Boom the agents are still working right here”Stream, 25 Oct, after quitting the game

Monitor · 7 of 8

### Glance down the hall

Status lamps show working, idle or interrupted. You see who needs you without opening anything.

“Every light that you see in there is an agent still working.”Stream, 28 Oct

Orchestrate · 7 of 8

### Walk the pipeline

One room per stage or team, so the shape of the work is visible to everyone who walks in.

“We just go to that room and just start building. And when we’re done, then we just leave that room.”Stream, 25 Oct

“So it’s like I’m spatially aware of my workspace. … It’s not a chat window, it’s an interface.”

First night of streaming the studio · 25 Oct 2026

05 / How we use it

## We run Omo Research from inside it, every day, live on stream.

Before we offer this to anyone, we use it ourselves. Our whole content studio is a row of rooms in one world. Each room is one stage, with its own agent profile and its own screens.

Room 1IdeasAgents gather and rank ideas for videos and posts.

Room 2ReferencesResearch and examples for the chosen idea.

Room 3RequirementsWhat to record, shot by shot.

Room 4EditingAgents cut and caption the footage.

Room 5PublishingA person reviews and approves here.

Room 6AnalyticsWhat worked, fed back into ideas.

MorningCome back to a world that kept working

After the PC had been off overnight, the world was exactly where we left it, and agents had edited 22 clips while we slept. I’m not dreading any pain or context loss.

Through the dayWalk the pipeline

Each piece of work moves from room to room. A video went through all five production rooms before a person saw it; the human’s job shrinks to reviewing and approving.

Any timeGlance down the hallway

Lamps outside each room show the state of the whole team from the doorway: working, idle or interrupted.

When the work changesAsk for a new room

Nobody places these blocks by hand. Our underground base and a robotics lab were each built by an agent from one prompt, live on stream. Was done in one shot. One prompt.

Hands freeTalk to an agent out loud

An agent player, Omo R1, joins the same world. You speak, a Hermes agent plans the job, and his body does it with 22 tools.

21–25sessions at once, at peak

22clips edited overnight

6rooms, one per stage

1prompt to build a room

06 / What runs at the desks

## The tools your teams already use, given a place.

Omo Space does not replace your agents. Every desk runs the real tool on a real machine, with your own model access.

Agents

### Hermes, Claude Code, Codex

Any desk can run Hermes Agent, Claude Code, Codex or a plain shell. Each Hermes desk can have its own profile, memory and skills.

Persistence

### Sessions that outlive the screen

Work keeps running when the screen closes, the game quits or the bridge restarts. After a reboot, desks reopen their tabs; nothing re-runs on its own.

Status

### Lamps and name plates

A name readable across the room, and a lamp that is lit while the agent works. The same signal can drive anything else in the world.

Web walls

### Live pages on the walls

Real browser pages for dashboards, docs and video, up to 12 in a world, each with its own tabs and sound.

Voice

### Agents with bodies

Agents on the same computer can join as players. Omo R1 takes spoken requests and acts in the world.

Research

### Robots in the same world

Open-source robots simulated with real physics walk on the blocks and come when called by voice. Early research, not a product.

07 / It travels

## A second person set it up in about a day.

A builder new to Hermes, working on Windows, set up his own world from the public repository and built an AI office in about a day, barely troubleshooting along the way. Unprompted, he said watching agents in a world was more fun than watching an AI type in a terminal.

“It just gave Claude the GitHub.”Second user, on stream · self-reported

08 / Built on research

## A forty-year-old idea, with live agents inside.

People remember where things are long after they forget names. Earlier systems arranged documents and windows, which sit still. We arrange agents that keep working, change state and ask questions while you are somewhere else.

1983DesksPiles remind people what to do.

1986RoomsVirtual workspaces end window thrashing.

1995Calm technologyKnow the state without looking.

1998Data MountainSpatial memory helps people find documents.

2026Omo SpaceRooms for live agents.

Sources and method in Rooms, Not Windows: seven stream recordings, about 29 hours, 791 quotes each checked word for word against the transcripts.

09 / What broke

## We show the failures too.

Five days of real use also broke things, on camera. Each failure is a design requirement, and each one shapes how we would run a pilot with you.

What happenedIn our studioWhat it means for a pilot

The 3D view crashedGame crashes and two whole-PC freezes. The agent sessions survived; the 3D client often did not.The work always lives outside the view. A crash costs you the picture, never the work.

A question was missedAn agent asked something and nothing told the builder. A lamp in another room is not a notification.Urgent questions need a backup that follows the person: a sound, a message, an alert.

Who is listening?With several voice agents in range, it was unclear which one was being spoken to.Voice needs a clear rule for who is addressed before teams share a space.

TrustThe second user would not use it at his day job, because an agent could delete a database.Permissions and review come before shared, multi-user spaces.

More is not betterA challenge to post 20 short videos in 100 minutes posted none.We measure the value of the work, not the volume of agents.

10 / Working with us

## Start with one team, one real workflow.

We work with a small number of organisations at a time. Each engagement starts from the work your people already do with agents, not from a demo.

### Map the work

We sit with one team and map how their agents run today: how many, which tools, where things get lost and who waits on whom.

### Build a pilot space

We design a space around that workflow: a room per stage or role, status everyone can see, and the agents your team already uses.

### Measure and decide

Your team uses it for real work. We write up what changed and what did not, in plain language, before anyone decides on more.

Measure 1 · FindTime to find a named agent

In the space versus your current tabs, at the number of agents your team really runs.

Measure 2 · ResumeTime back to useful work

After a break or a day away, how long until the first useful action.

Measure 3 · MonitorTime to notice a stuck agent

How long an agent waits on a question before someone sees it.

These are the tests proposed in our working paper. A pilot is how we find out whether the effect holds for your teams, or not.

11 / Where it fits

## For teams that already run many agents.

Content and creative: one room per stage, from idea to publish. This is how we run our own channels.

Research and engineering: rooms where papers, experiments and long runs stay on the walls while people move between them.

New interfaces: agents that join the world as players you can talk to. Early research.

12 / Security and honesty

## What it is today, and what it is not yet.

Our motto is questions before claims. Here is the plain version, so nobody is surprised in a security review.

- Local by design. The bridge listens on this machine only (127.0.0.1) and refuses foreign hosts. Worlds store workspace ids, never a credential.

- Your models, your permissions. Agents use your own model access and keep their own approval prompts. Nothing turns on paid inference by itself.

- Not a sandbox. A room is a way to see work, not a security boundary. Agents have the same access as a terminal.

- Single machine today. Workspaces live on the PC that opened them. Shared, multi-user spaces are part of what pilots explore.

- Not yet built: single sign-on, an admin console, audit exports. Tested end to end on Linux; macOS and Windows support is newer. Security notes ↗

13 / Talk to us

## Tell us how your teams work with agents.

A short form. We read every request ourselves and reply with a time to talk, or an honest note if we are not the right fit yet.

- A 30-minute conversationAbout your teams, your agents and what slows them down.

- No slides, no pressureWe show the real system running, in our own studio.

- Prefer email?harrythentrepreneur@gmail.com

Questions

Do our people need to play Minecraft?

No game skills are needed. You walk, look and type. Today's system uses Minecraft as the view because it is a fast way to build and walk through spaces, and agents can build it for you. What we study is the interface: places, presence and status, not the game.

Why Minecraft, for a serious organisation?

It is already multiplayer, already buildable and familiar to a generation of people, and the world itself can be written by agents, which earlier 3D desktops could not do. The cost is a client that is heavier and less reliable than a terminal, which is why the work never lives inside it.

Which agents does it work with?

Any desk can run Hermes Agent, Claude Code, Codex or a plain shell. They are the real tools, running on your machine, with your own model access.

Does it replace our existing tools?

No. Your agents, repositories and dashboards stay where they are. The space is a way to see and reach them; web walls can show the dashboards you already use.

Is our data sent to you?

No. The open-source system runs on your machine and talks to nothing of ours. If we work together on a pilot, what we see is agreed with you first.

What does it cost?

The core is free and open source. Pilots are scoped per organisation after a first conversation.

Your teams now run dozens. Let's find out together what a place does for them.
